When they saw what had happened of the great stoning and the prevention of eavesdropping, they said: ﴿We do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth﴾, which is their disbelief in this Prophet ﷺ, so that evil would befall them, ﴿or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance﴾, so that they would believe in him and be guided. When they mentioned evil, they did not attribute it to God, exalted is He; when they mentioned guidance, they attributed it to Him, exalted is He.

﴿And that among us are the righteous﴾: they informed of what they were upon of righteousness and otherwise.

﴿And among us are those below that﴾: that is, below the righteous. "Dūna" occurs in places where "ghayr" would occur, so it is as if he said: "and among us are non-righteous." It is also permitted that they meant: "and among us are those below that in righteousness," that is, among them are the pious, and among them are those who are not complete in righteousness. "Dūna" is in the position of an attribute of an omitted noun, meaning: "and among us are a people below that." This omitted described noun may be dropped in the division with "min," even in clauses; they say: "Among us are those who departed, and among us are those who stayed," meaning: "among us is a group that departed, and among us is a group that stayed." The clause ﴿we were paths, separate groups﴾ is an explanation of the earlier division. Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, and Qatada said: divergent desires; it was also said: divergent sects. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, we were people of divergent ways, or we were in our divergent conditions like divergent paths, or we were on divergent paths, as in His saying: "as the fox made the path [smooth]," or our paths were qidad, with the omission of the mudaf which is "paths" and the mudaf ilayhi (the pronoun) standing in its place. End of quote. In his first two estimates, the omission is of the mudaf from "paths" and the mudaf ilayhi standing in its place, since he omitted "possessors of" and "like." As for the third estimate, that it be accusative by dropping "fi" (in), this is not permitted except in necessity, and Sibawayh explicitly stated that ʿasala al-ṭarīq is anomalous, so the Qur'an is not to be construed upon it.

﴿And that we thought that we would not frustrate God﴾: that is, we were certain ﴿in the earth﴾: that is, existing in the earth ﴿and we would not frustrate Him by flight﴾: that is, from the earth to the heaven. "Fi al-ard" and "haraban" are two ḥāls, that is, fleeing or fugitives.

﴿And that when we heard the guidance﴾: which is the Qur'an ﴿we believed in it﴾: that is, in the Qur'an ﴿so whoever believes in his Lord will not fear﴾: that is, he does not fear. Ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, and the majority read ﴿fa-lā yakhāfu﴾, and their reading is taken as a negation. It was also said: the fa' is extra and there is no negation. This is not correct. The answer with fa' was better than bringing the verb in the jussive without fa', because when it is with fa' it is by way of an implied subject, that is: "so he does not fear." The nominal clause is more indicative and more emphatic than the verbal clause in establishing the content of the clause. (bakhsan) Ibn ʿAbbas said: the diminishing of good deeds; ﴿nor any injustice﴾ he said: an increase in bad deeds; ﴿nor any injustice﴾ it was said: the imposition of what cannot be borne. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, a recompense of diminution or injustice; because he diminishes no one's right and does not commit injustice against anyone, so he does not fear the recompense of either. It is also permitted that it be meant: "so he does not fear that he will be diminished, but he will be rewarded with the fullest reward, nor that disgrace will overtake him," from His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿disgrace will overtake them﴾ [al-Qalam: 43]. End of quote.

The majority read (bakhsan) with sukun on the kha'. Ibn Thabit read it with fatha.

﴿And among us are the qasitun﴾: that is, the disbelievers who deviate from the truth. Mujahid and Qatada said: "qasit" is the wrongdoer, the unjust; and from this is the verse of the poet:

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 72, verses 1–15 (part 3 of 3)**

A verse of poetry:

*"A people who killed the son of Hind by force,*
*and who were unjust to al-Nu'man."*

This division came, although it had already been mentioned in ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that﴾, to mention the condition of the two groups, those who are saved and those who are destroyed, and to encourage whoever enters Islam. The apparent meaning is that ﴿Whoever submits﴾ up to the end of the two conditions is part of the speech of the jinn. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The better view is that ﴿Whoever submits﴾ is an address from God Most High to Muhammad (ﷺ), and the verses that follow support this."

al-A'raj recited *rushdan* (رُشْدًا) with a *damma* on the *ra'* and a *sukun* on the *shin*. The majority recite it with a *fatha* on both. al-Zamakhshari said: "Someone who does not hold that the jinn receive reward has claimed that God Most High threatened their unjust ones but did not promise reward to their Muslims, and that is threat enough." That is, *fa-ulā'ika taharraw rashadan* (فَأُولَئِكَ تَحَرَّوْا رَشَدًا), so he mentioned the cause of the reward and what makes it due, and God is too just to punish the unjust while not rewarding the rightly guided. End of quotation. In it there is a hidden insinuation (*dasisah*) of Mu'tazilism (the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, a rationalist theological school) in his phrase "and what makes it due."

[p. 344]

**Surat al-Jinn is Meccan and has twenty-eight verses.**

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened and said: "We have heard a wondrous Qur'an,﴾ ﴿guiding to right conduct, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord.﴾ ﴿And that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, has taken neither a consort nor a son.﴾ ﴿And that our foolish one used to speak against God with outrageous falsehood.﴾ ﴿And that we had thought that humans and jinn would never tell lies about God.﴾ ﴿And that some men of mankind used to seek refuge with some men of the jinn, so they increased them in distress.﴾ ﴿And that they thought, as you thought, that God would never raise anyone up.﴾ ﴿And that we touched the heaven and found it filled with severe guards and meteors.﴾ ﴿And that we used to sit in some of its places to listen, but whoever listens now finds a watching meteor lying in wait for him.﴾ ﴿And that we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance.﴾ ﴿And that among us are the righteous, and among us are others below that; we were of divers ways.﴾ ﴿And that we thought we could not escape God on earth, nor could we escape Him by flight.﴾ ﴿And that when we heard the guidance, we believed in it; so whoever believes in his Lord fears neither loss nor distress.﴾ ﴿And that among us are the Muslims, and among us are the deviators. Whoever submits, those have sought out right guidance.﴾ ﴿But as for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell.﴾ ﴿And that if they had remained upright on the path, We would have given them abundant water to drink.﴾ ﴿That We might test them therein. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And that the mosques belong to God, so do not call upon anyone along with God.﴾ ﴿And that when the servant of God stood calling upon Him, they nearly became a crowd pressing upon him.﴾ ﴿Say: I only call upon my Lord and I associate no one with Him.﴾ ﴿Say: I do not control for you any harm or any right guidance.﴾ ﴿Say: No one can protect me from God, nor will I find any refuge besides Him.﴾ ﴿Except a message from God and His messages. And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever.﴾ ﴿Until, when they see what they are promised, they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number.﴾ ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will appoint for it a long term.﴾ ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone,﴾ ﴿except a messenger whom He has chosen; for indeed He sends before him and behind him a guard,﴾ ﴿that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord. And He encompasses what is with them and has counted everything in number.﴾

[p. 345]

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened and said: "We have heard a wondrous Qur'an,﴾ ... ﴿and as for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell.﴾

[p. 346]

This surah is Meccan. Its connection with what precedes it is this: when God related the persistence of the people of Noah in disbelief and their devotion to idol worship, and Noah (peace be upon him) was the first messenger to the earth, just as Muhammad (ﷺ) is the last messenger to the earth, and the Arabs, of whom he (peace be upon him) was one, were worshippers of idols like the people of Noah, to the point that they worshipped idols similar to those in name, and what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought of the Qur'an was a guide to right conduct, and the Arabs had heard it, yet most of them hesitated to believe in it, God revealed Surat al-Jinn immediately after Surat Nuh, as a rebuke to the Quraysh and the Arabs for their slowness to believe, since the jinn were better than them and more receptive to belief, even though they were not of the same kind as the Messenger (ﷺ). Yet by merely hearing the Qur'an, they were overawed by it and believed in it at once, and they knew that it was not of the pattern of human speech. By contrast, the Arabs, although it was revealed in their tongue and they recognised that it was inimitable, denied it and those who brought it out of envy and insolence, that God should send down His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read ﴿qul uhiya﴾ with four radicals (uhiya, passive of aha). Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Ataki, from Abu Amr, and Abu Unas Juwayya ibn A'idh al-Asadi read (wuhiya) with three radicals. It is said: waha and awha have the same meaning. Al-Ajjaj said:

*He drew to her the settled ground, and she settled.*

Zayd ibn Ali and Juwayya, as transmitted from al-Kisa'i and Ibn Abi Ablah also, read (uhiya) by replacing the waw with a hamza, just as they said in (wa'ada) (he promised): (a'ada). Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is from the unrestricted interchange (al-qalb al-mutlaq), whose permissibility applies to every waw that is pronounced with damma." End of quotation. It is not as he mentioned; rather, there is detail here, namely that the waw with damma may occur initially, medially, or finally, and each has its own rules, and some of these are disputed and detailed in grammar. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-Mazini applied this even to the kasra, as in (ishah) and (isadah) and (i'a akhihi)." End of quotation. This is exaggeration and showing off. He used to mention this in ﴿wi'a akhihi﴾ [Yusuf 76] in the surah of Yusuf. Al-Mazini had two opinions on this: one, that it is by analogy as he said; the other, that it is restricted to what is heard (samā').

The phrase ﴿annahu istama'a﴾ is in the position of the object of the passive verb, i.e., the listening (istima') of "a company of the jinn." The well-known view is that this listening is the one mentioned in al-Ahqaf in God's words: ﴿And when We turned towards you a company of the jinn who listened to the Qur'an﴾ [al-Ahqaf 29], and it is one single incident. It is also said there were two incidents: the jinn who came to him in Mecca were the jinn of Nasibin, and those who came to him at Nakhla were the jinn of Nineveh. As for the surah they heard, Ikrima said it was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-Alaq 1]. It was also said it was Surat al-Rahman. The verse does not address, neither here nor in al-Ahqaf, whether he saw them and spoke to them (peace be upon him). What appears from the hadith is that it happened twice. The first was at the beginning of the prophetic mission of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), at the time when Abdullah ibn Mas'ud reported that he was not with him on the night of the jinn. They had lost him (peace be upon him), and they searched for him in the valleys and ravines but did not find him. When morning came, behold, he came from the direction of Hira. In it: "The caller of the jinn came to me, so I went with him (p. 347) and recited the Qur'an to them. He set out with us and showed us their traces and the traces of their fires." The second time, Ibn Mas'ud was with him. The Prophet (ﷺ) had called upon anyone to accompany him to recite the Qur'an to the jinn, but no one rose except Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. He went with him to al-Hajun near the ravine. He drew a line for him and said: "Do not cross it." Then there descended upon him (peace be upon him) like stones, they dragged the stones with their feet, walking and beating their drums as women beat their tambourines, until they covered him, and I could no longer see him, so I stood up. He signalled to me with his hand to sit. He recited the Qur'an, and his voice kept rising, and they vanished into the earth until I could no longer see them." The hadith. That these were two incidents is shown by their disagreement about the number: it was said seven, and it was said nine. From Zirr: they were three from the people of Harran and four from the people of Nasibin, a town in Yemen other than the town in Iraq. From Ikrima: they were twelve thousand from the island of Mosul. And where are seven out of twelve thousand?

﴿So they said: "We have heard a wondrous Qur'an"﴾. That is, they said to their people when they returned to them, and they described (Qur'anan) by saying (ajaban), describing it with the verbal noun as an intensification, meaning: it is wondrous in itself, for the eloquence of its speech, the goodness of its structures, the subtlety of its meanings, the strangeness of its style, the eloquence of its admonitions, and its being unlike all other books. And 'ajab (wonder) is what departs from any of its forms and analogues.

﴿Guiding to right conduct﴾: that is, it calls to what is correct. It is also said: to monotheism and faith. Al-Jumhur read (al-rushd) with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the shin. Isa read both with damma. Also from him: both with fatha.

﴿So we have believed in it﴾: that is, in the Qur'an. Since belief in it includes belief in God and in His oneness and freedom from polytheism, they said: ﴿and we will never associate anyone with our Lord﴾. The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi', of Mecca and Medina) and the two Abus read with fatha the hamza in His words ﴿wa-annahu ta'ala﴾ and what follows it, twelve verses, the last of which is ﴿wa-anna minna al-muslimun﴾. The remaining seven read with kasra. As for the kasra, it is clear, because these are conjoined to His words ﴿inna sami'na﴾, so they are included within the object of the saying. As for the fatha, Abu Hatim said: it is governed by (uhiya), so all of it is in the position of nominative as the object not named as agent. End of quotation. This is not correct, because among the conjoined elements is that which cannot be included under (uhiya), namely whatever contains the first-person pronoun, as in His words: ﴿And that we used to sit in some of its places to listen﴾. Do you not see that it does not fit with ﴿It has been revealed to me﴾ followed by ﴿that we used to sit in some of its places﴾? And the same applies to the rest. The reading with fatha is explained as follows: all these are conjoined to the pronoun governed by the preposition in (bihi) in His words ﴿so we have believed in it﴾, meaning "and [we believed] that He..." and so on for the rest. This is permissible according to the Kufans' view, and it is the correct view. We have already argued for the validity of this in His words ﴿and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah 217]. Makki said: it is better in that the omission of the preposition before (anna) is more frequent in the rest. Al-Zajjaj said: its explanation is that it is treated as governed by (amanna bihi), because its meaning is: "we accepted it and knew it," so the meaning becomes: "so we believed in it, that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord..." Al-Farra' preceded him in a similar view, saying: "(anna) is read with fatha because belief falls upon it. You will find that belief is fitting in some of what is read with fatha and not in others, but that does not prevent you from keeping them all with fatha, for what necessitates fatha of (anna) fits there, such as (we affirmed) and (we testified)."

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 72, verses 1–15 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Farra' pointed out that some of what has been given the fatha does not fit with governing "āmannā" over it, such as His saying: ﴿And that we thought that mankind and the jinn would never speak a lie against God﴾. Al-Zamakhshari followed them both and said: "As for whoever gave all of them the fatha, it is by way of conjunction with the place of the prepositional phrase in ﴿we believed in it﴾, as if it were said: 'We affirmed it, and we affirmed that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, and that he [i.e., the foolish one among us] used to say...' and likewise the rest." End of quote. He did not perceive what al-Farra' perceived, namely that some of them cannot properly be governed by (āmannā).

The majority read ﴿jadd rabbinā﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a damma on the dal, in construct with "rabbinā," meaning: His majesty (ʿaẓamatuhu). This is the view of the majority. Anas and al-Hasan said: His wealth/sufficiency (ghināhu). Mujahid said: His mention (dhikruhu). Ibn ʿAbbas said: His rank and His command (qadruhu wa amruhu). ʿIkrima read (jaddun) with tanwin, (rabbunā) in the nominative, as if he said: "He is great, our Lord," so "rabbunā" is a substitute (badal). Al-jadd in the language means "the great." Humayd ibn Qays read jaddun with a damma on the jim, in construct, and its meaning is "the great," transmitted by Sibawayh; it is an idafa of the attribute to the thing described, and the meaning is: "Exalted is our Lord, the Great." ʿIkrima also read jaddan rabbunā, with fatha on the jim and dal, tanwin, and raising of "rabbunā," with jaddan in the accusative as a tamyiz transferred from the subject; its origin is "Exalted is the majesty of our Lord." Qatada and ʿIkrima also read jiddan with kasra on the jim and tanwin, in the accusative, with "rabbunā" raised. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: jiddan is accusative as a ḥāl, and its meaning is: "exalted in truth and in power." Others said: it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, its estimate being: "ta'ālayā jiddan," and rabbunā is nominative by taʿālā. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ read jaddayi rabbinā, meaning: His bounty and benefit. The majority read ﴿yaqūlu safīhunā﴾: it is Iblis. It was also said: it is a collective noun for every fool, and Iblis is the leader of the fools. Al-shatat means transgression and going beyond the due measure. Al-A'sha said:
Will they desist, when he will not forbid those of excess, / like a spear-thrust from which oil and wick flow out.
It is said: "ashatta fi al-sawm" when one goes far in the bargain, meaning: a statement which is in itself excess, which is the attribution of a consort and a son to God, exalted is He.

﴿And that we thought﴾ the verse: that is, we had thought well of mankind and the jinn, and we believed that no one would dare to lie against God by attributing to Him a consort and a son. So we believed in the truth of what Iblis and his rebels had led us astray with, until we heard the Qur'an and clarified their lie.

The majority read ﴿an lan taqūla﴾, the imperfect of qāla. Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra, Yaʿqub, and Ibn Miqsam read taqawwala, the imperfect of tataqawwalu, with one of the two tas omitted. In the majority reading, "kadhiban" is accusative by "taqūla," because a lie is a kind of speech, or it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: "a speech, a lie," i.e., a fabricated speech. In the anomalous reading it is a verbal noun of "taqūla," since it is itself lying, so it is like "qa'adtu juluusan" (I sat sitting).

﴿And that there were men﴾. The majority narrated that a man, when he wished to spend the night or settle in a valley, would call out at the top of his voice: "O Master of this valley! I seek refuge in you from the foolish ones who are in your obedience," believing that the jinni in the valley would protect and shield him. It is reported that the jinn would then say: "We possess neither for you nor for ourselves anything from God." Muqatil said: The first people to seek refuge with the jinn were a people from Yemen, then the Banu Hanifa, then this spread among the Arabs. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun subject in (fa-zādūhum) refers to ﴿men from mankind﴾, since they are the ones spoken of; this is the view of Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr. (fa-zādūhum): that is, mankind increased them (rahaqan): that is, audacity, arrogance, insolence, transgression, and committing what is forbidden, and self-admiration, to the extent that they said: "We have mastered mankind and the jinn." Some explained rahaq as sin. Al-Tabari cited the verse of al-A'sha on this:
Nothing benefits me apart from seeing her; / the lover is not healed unless he has been struck with rahaq.
He said its meaning: "unless he has committed the forbidden." The meaning is: mankind increased the jinn in sin, because they glorified them, so they increased them in permitting themselves the prohibitions of God, exalted is He. Qatada, Abu al-ʿAliya, al-Rabiʿ, and Ibn Zayd said: (fa-zādūhum): that is, the jinn increased mankind in fear, imagining to them to the utmost of their ability, and misleading them, since they saw the lightness of their judgment, so they despised and belittled them. Ibn Jubayr said: (rahaqan) means disbelief. It was also said: the word "rijāl" is not applied to the jinn, so the meaning is: "And there were men from mankind who sought refuge from the evil of the jinn with men from mankind," and a man would say, for example: "I seek refuge with Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman from the jinn of this valley." This is a strange view.

(And that they) that is, the disbelievers of mankind ﴿thought as you thought﴾, O jinn, addressing one another. Both "thought" and "you thought" each require ﴿that God would not raise up﴾, so the matter is one of tanāzuʿ (operating on a common complement), and "an" here is the lightened form of the heavy "anna." It was also said: the pronoun in (and that they) refers to the jinn, and the address in "you thought" is to Quraysh, and this and the one before it are from what is revealed, not from the speech of the jinn: ﴿that God would never raise up anyone﴾: the apparent meaning is the sending of a messenger to creation, and this is most fitting to what precedes and follows the verses. It was also said: the resurrection.

﴿And that we touched the heaven﴾: the original meaning of lams is touch; then it was used figuratively for seeking, and the meaning is: we sought to reach the heaven in order to listen to the speech of its inhabitants, and we found it filled. The apparent meaning is that "wajada" here means "encountered and found," and it took one object, and the clause "mulli'at" is in the position of a ḥāl. It was also permitted that it take two objects, with (fa-mulli'at) in the position of the second object. al-A'raj read mulīyat with ya without hamza; the majority read with hamza. And shadīdan is an attribute of al-ḥaras according to the wording, because it is a collective noun, as he said:
I fear a little rujayl or a little rukayb, a hostile one.
Were the meaning observed, he would say shiddādan in the plural. The apparent meaning of al-ḥaras is the angels, that is, guarding against the devils approaching it, and shuhuban is the plural of shihab, which is what the devils are pelted with when they listen. It was said: it is possible that the shuhub are the ḥaras; the meaning is repeated when the wording differs, as in:
And Hind—between her and me there came distance and remoteness.
His saying: ﴿we found it filled﴾ indicates that previously they used to sneak into the heaven and did not find it filled. (maqā'id) is the plural of maq'ad, and the Messenger of God ﷺ explained the form of the jinn's sitting: "They were one above another, and whenever the upper one was burned, the one beneath him rose into his place. They would steal a word and throw it to the soothsayers, adding to it, and then the soothsayers would add to the word a hundred lies."

﴿Now whoever listens﴾: "al-ān" is a time adverb for the present, and "yastamiʿu" is in the future; the adverb was stretched and used for the future, as he said:
I will strive now, when its limit is reached.
The meaning is: whoever among them listens in the coming time ﴿will find for himself a watching flame﴾, that is, one who watches for him and burns him. This is for whoever listens. As for hearing, it has ceased, as God said: ﴿Indeed they are cut off from hearing﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 212]. The stoning was in the Jahiliyya, and that is mentioned in their poetry, and the hadith indicates it when he, peace be upon him, saw a star that had been shot down, and said: "What did you used to say about such a thing in the Jahiliyya?" They said: "We used to say: a great one dies or a great one is born." Aws ibn Hajar said:
It leapt like a pearl, followed by / a dust cloud rising, you would think it a tent-rope.
ʿAwf ibn al-Jaz' said:
So he returned to us the caravan, apart from its mate, / or the bull like a pearl, followed by blood.
Bishr ibn Abi Hazim said:
The caravan is overtaken by dust, and its foal / darts after the two like the darting of a star.
Al-Tibrizi said: all these poets are Jahiliyya; there is none among them who was a mukhadram. Ma'mar said: I said to al-Zuhri: "Were stars shot at in the Jahiliyya?" He said: "Yes." I said: "What do you say about His saying: ﴿and that we used to sit in it in places for listening﴾?" He said: "Its matter was made severe and intensified when the Messenger of God was sent." Al-Jahiz said: the view that it was shooting is more correct, because of His saying: ﴿we found it filled﴾, and this is information from the jinn that the guard of the heaven was increased until it was filled, and because of what Ibn ʿAbbas narrated, and he mentioned the earlier hadith. Al-Zamakhshari, following al-Jahiz, said: in His saying is proof that the ḥaras is fullness and abundance, therefore ﴿we used to sit in it in places﴾, that is, we used to find some of the places empty of guards and meteors, and now all the places are filled. End of quote. All of this refutes the view of those who say that the stoning occurred after the mission of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and that it was one of his signs. The apparent meaning of "rasadan" is: "possessors of a meteor, watching with the stoning," and they are the angels who pelt them with shooting stars and prevent them from listening.

When they saw what had happened of the great stoning and the prevention of eavesdropping, they said: ﴿We do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth﴾, which is their disbelief in this Prophet ﷺ, so that evil would befall them, ﴿or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance﴾, so that they would believe in him and be guided. When they mentioned evil, they did not attribute it to God, exalted is He; when they mentioned guidance, they attributed it to Him, exalted is He.

﴿And that among us are the righteous﴾: they informed of what they were upon of righteousness and otherwise.

﴿And among us are those below that﴾: that is, below the righteous. "Dūna" occurs in places where "ghayr" would occur, so it is as if he said: "and among us are non-righteous." It is also permitted that they meant: "and among us are those below that in righteousness," that is, among them are the pious, and among them are those who are not complete in righteousness. "Dūna" is in the position of an attribute of an omitted noun, meaning: "and among us are a people below that." This omitted described noun may be dropped in the division with "min," even in clauses; they say: "Among us are those who departed, and among us are those who stayed," meaning: "among us is a group that departed, and among us is a group that stayed." The clause ﴿we were paths, separate groups﴾ is an explanation of the earlier division. Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, and Qatada said: divergent desires; it was also said: divergent sects. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, we were people of divergent ways, or we were in our divergent conditions like divergent paths, or we were on divergent paths, as in His saying: "as the fox made the path [smooth]," or our paths were qidad, with the omission of the mudaf which is "paths" and the mudaf ilayhi (the pronoun) standing in its place. End of quote. In his first two estimates, the omission is of the mudaf from "paths" and the mudaf ilayhi standing in its place, since he omitted "possessors of" and "like." As for the third estimate, that it be accusative by dropping "fi" (in), this is not permitted except in necessity, and Sibawayh explicitly stated that ʿasala al-ṭarīq is anomalous, so the Qur'an is not to be construed upon it.

﴿And that we thought that we would not frustrate God﴾: that is, we were certain ﴿in the earth﴾: that is, existing in the earth ﴿and we would not frustrate Him by flight﴾: that is, from the earth to the heaven. "Fi al-ard" and "haraban" are two ḥāls, that is, fleeing or fugitives.

﴿And that when we heard the guidance﴾: which is the Qur'an ﴿we believed in it﴾: that is, in the Qur'an ﴿so whoever believes in his Lord will not fear﴾: that is, he does not fear. Ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, and the majority read ﴿fa-lā yakhāfu﴾, and their reading is taken as a negation. It was also said: the fa' is extra and there is no negation. This is not correct. The answer with fa' was better than bringing the verb in the jussive without fa', because when it is with fa' it is by way of an implied subject, that is: "so he does not fear." The nominal clause is more indicative and more emphatic than the verbal clause in establishing the content of the clause. (bakhsan) Ibn ʿAbbas said: the diminishing of good deeds; ﴿nor any injustice﴾ he said: an increase in bad deeds; ﴿nor any injustice﴾ it was said: the imposition of what cannot be borne. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, a recompense of diminution or injustice; because he diminishes no one's right and does not commit injustice against anyone, so he does not fear the recompense of either. It is also permitted that it be meant: "so he does not fear that he will be diminished, but he will be rewarded with the fullest reward, nor that disgrace will overtake him," from His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿disgrace will overtake them﴾ [al-Qalam: 43]. End of quote.

The majority read (bakhsan) with sukun on the kha'. Ibn Thabit read it with fatha.

﴿And among us are the qasitun﴾: that is, the disbelievers who deviate from the truth. Mujahid and Qatada said: "qasit" is the wrongdoer, the unjust; and from this is the verse of the poet:

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 72, verses 1–15 (part 3 of 3)**

A verse of poetry:

*"A people who killed the son of Hind by force,*
*and who were unjust to al-Nu'man."*

This division came, although it had already been mentioned in ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that﴾, to mention the condition of the two groups, those who are saved and those who are destroyed, and to encourage whoever enters Islam. The apparent meaning is that ﴿Whoever submits﴾ up to the end of the two conditions is part of the speech of the jinn. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The better view is that ﴿Whoever submits﴾ is an address from God Most High to Muhammad (ﷺ), and the verses that follow support this."

al-A'raj recited *rushdan* (رُشْدًا) with a *damma* on the *ra'* and a *sukun* on the *shin*. The majority recite it with a *fatha* on both. al-Zamakhshari said: "Someone who does not hold that the jinn receive reward has claimed that God Most High threatened their unjust ones but did not promise reward to their Muslims, and that is threat enough." That is, *fa-ulā'ika taharraw rashadan* (فَأُولَئِكَ تَحَرَّوْا رَشَدًا), so he mentioned the cause of the reward and what makes it due, and God is too just to punish the unjust while not rewarding the rightly guided. End of quotation. In it there is a hidden insinuation (*dasisah*) of Mu'tazilism (the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, a rationalist theological school) in his phrase "and what makes it due."

[p. 344]

**Surat al-Jinn is Meccan and has twenty-eight verses.**

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened and said: "We have heard a wondrous Qur'an,﴾ ﴿guiding to right conduct, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord.﴾ ﴿And that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, has taken neither a consort nor a son.﴾ ﴿And that our foolish one used to speak against God with outrageous falsehood.﴾ ﴿And that we had thought that humans and jinn would never tell lies about God.﴾ ﴿And that some men of mankind used to seek refuge with some men of the jinn, so they increased them in distress.﴾ ﴿And that they thought, as you thought, that God would never raise anyone up.﴾ ﴿And that we touched the heaven and found it filled with severe guards and meteors.﴾ ﴿And that we used to sit in some of its places to listen, but whoever listens now finds a watching meteor lying in wait for him.﴾ ﴿And that we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance.﴾ ﴿And that among us are the righteous, and among us are others below that; we were of divers ways.﴾ ﴿And that we thought we could not escape God on earth, nor could we escape Him by flight.﴾ ﴿And that when we heard the guidance, we believed in it; so whoever believes in his Lord fears neither loss nor distress.﴾ ﴿And that among us are the Muslims, and among us are the deviators. Whoever submits, those have sought out right guidance.﴾ ﴿But as for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell.﴾ ﴿And that if they had remained upright on the path, We would have given them abundant water to drink.﴾ ﴿That We might test them therein. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And that the mosques belong to God, so do not call upon anyone along with God.﴾ ﴿And that when the servant of God stood calling upon Him, they nearly became a crowd pressing upon him.﴾ ﴿Say: I only call upon my Lord and I associate no one with Him.﴾ ﴿Say: I do not control for you any harm or any right guidance.﴾ ﴿Say: No one can protect me from God, nor will I find any refuge besides Him.﴾ ﴿Except a message from God and His messages. And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever.﴾ ﴿Until, when they see what they are promised, they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number.﴾ ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will appoint for it a long term.﴾ ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone,﴾ ﴿except a messenger whom He has chosen; for indeed He sends before him and behind him a guard,﴾ ﴿that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord. And He encompasses what is with them and has counted everything in number.﴾

[p. 345]

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened and said: "We have heard a wondrous Qur'an,﴾ ... ﴿and as for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell.﴾

[p. 346]

This surah is Meccan. Its connection with what precedes it is this: when God related the persistence of the people of Noah in disbelief and their devotion to idol worship, and Noah (peace be upon him) was the first messenger to the earth, just as Muhammad (ﷺ) is the last messenger to the earth, and the Arabs, of whom he (peace be upon him) was one, were worshippers of idols like the people of Noah, to the point that they worshipped idols similar to those in name, and what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought of the Qur'an was a guide to right conduct, and the Arabs had heard it, yet most of them hesitated to believe in it, God revealed Surat al-Jinn immediately after Surat Nuh, as a rebuke to the Quraysh and the Arabs for their slowness to believe, since the jinn were better than them and more receptive to belief, even though they were not of the same kind as the Messenger (ﷺ). Yet by merely hearing the Qur'an, they were overawed by it and believed in it at once, and they knew that it was not of the pattern of human speech. By contrast, the Arabs, although it was revealed in their tongue and they recognised that it was inimitable, denied it and those who brought it out of envy and insolence, that God should send down His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read ﴿qul uhiya﴾ with four radicals (uhiya, passive of aha). Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Ataki, from Abu Amr, and Abu Unas Juwayya ibn A'idh al-Asadi read (wuhiya) with three radicals. It is said: waha and awha have the same meaning. Al-Ajjaj said:

*He drew to her the settled ground, and she settled.*

Zayd ibn Ali and Juwayya, as transmitted from al-Kisa'i and Ibn Abi Ablah also, read (uhiya) by replacing the waw with a hamza, just as they said in (wa'ada) (he promised): (a'ada). Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is from the unrestricted interchange (al-qalb al-mutlaq), whose permissibility applies to every waw that is pronounced with damma." End of quotation. It is not as he mentioned; rather, there is detail here, namely that the waw with damma may occur initially, medially, or finally, and each has its own rules, and some of these are disputed and detailed in grammar. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-Mazini applied this even to the kasra, as in (ishah) and (isadah) and (i'a akhihi)." End of quotation. This is exaggeration and showing off. He used to mention this in ﴿wi'a akhihi﴾ [Yusuf 76] in the surah of Yusuf. Al-Mazini had two opinions on this: one, that it is by analogy as he said; the other, that it is restricted to what is heard (samā').

The phrase ﴿annahu istama'a﴾ is in the position of the object of the passive verb, i.e., the listening (istima') of "a company of the jinn." The well-known view is that this listening is the one mentioned in al-Ahqaf in God's words: ﴿And when We turned towards you a company of the jinn who listened to the Qur'an﴾ [al-Ahqaf 29], and it is one single incident. It is also said there were two incidents: the jinn who came to him in Mecca were the jinn of Nasibin, and those who came to him at Nakhla were the jinn of Nineveh. As for the surah they heard, Ikrima said it was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-Alaq 1]. It was also said it was Surat al-Rahman. The verse does not address, neither here nor in al-Ahqaf, whether he saw them and spoke to them (peace be upon him). What appears from the hadith is that it happened twice. The first was at the beginning of the prophetic mission of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), at the time when Abdullah ibn Mas'ud reported that he was not with him on the night of the jinn. They had lost him (peace be upon him), and they searched for him in the valleys and ravines but did not find him. When morning came, behold, he came from the direction of Hira. In it: "The caller of the jinn came to me, so I went with him (p. 347) and recited the Qur'an to them. He set out with us and showed us their traces and the traces of their fires." The second time, Ibn Mas'ud was with him. The Prophet (ﷺ) had called upon anyone to accompany him to recite the Qur'an to the jinn, but no one rose except Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. He went with him to al-Hajun near the ravine. He drew a line for him and said: "Do not cross it." Then there descended upon him (peace be upon him) like stones, they dragged the stones with their feet, walking and beating their drums as women beat their tambourines, until they covered him, and I could no longer see him, so I stood up. He signalled to me with his hand to sit. He recited the Qur'an, and his voice kept rising, and they vanished into the earth until I could no longer see them." The hadith. That these were two incidents is shown by their disagreement about the number: it was said seven, and it was said nine. From Zirr: they were three from the people of Harran and four from the people of Nasibin, a town in Yemen other than the town in Iraq. From Ikrima: they were twelve thousand from the island of Mosul. And where are seven out of twelve thousand?

﴿So they said: "We have heard a wondrous Qur'an"﴾. That is, they said to their people when they returned to them, and they described (Qur'anan) by saying (ajaban), describing it with the verbal noun as an intensification, meaning: it is wondrous in itself, for the eloquence of its speech, the goodness of its structures, the subtlety of its meanings, the strangeness of its style, the eloquence of its admonitions, and its being unlike all other books. And 'ajab (wonder) is what departs from any of its forms and analogues.

﴿Guiding to right conduct﴾: that is, it calls to what is correct. It is also said: to monotheism and faith. Al-Jumhur read (al-rushd) with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the shin. Isa read both with damma. Also from him: both with fatha.

﴿So we have believed in it﴾: that is, in the Qur'an. Since belief in it includes belief in God and in His oneness and freedom from polytheism, they said: ﴿and we will never associate anyone with our Lord﴾. The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi', of Mecca and Medina) and the two Abus read with fatha the hamza in His words ﴿wa-annahu ta'ala﴾ and what follows it, twelve verses, the last of which is ﴿wa-anna minna al-muslimun﴾. The remaining seven read with kasra. As for the kasra, it is clear, because these are conjoined to His words ﴿inna sami'na﴾, so they are included within the object of the saying. As for the fatha, Abu Hatim said: it is governed by (uhiya), so all of it is in the position of nominative as the object not named as agent. End of quotation. This is not correct, because among the conjoined elements is that which cannot be included under (uhiya), namely whatever contains the first-person pronoun, as in His words: ﴿And that we used to sit in some of its places to listen﴾. Do you not see that it does not fit with ﴿It has been revealed to me﴾ followed by ﴿that we used to sit in some of its places﴾? And the same applies to the rest. The reading with fatha is explained as follows: all these are conjoined to the pronoun governed by the preposition in (bihi) in His words ﴿so we have believed in it﴾, meaning "and [we believed] that He..." and so on for the rest. This is permissible according to the Kufans' view, and it is the correct view. We have already argued for the validity of this in His words ﴿and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah 217]. Makki said: it is better in that the omission of the preposition before (anna) is more frequent in the rest. Al-Zajjaj said: its explanation is that it is treated as governed by (amanna bihi), because its meaning is: "we accepted it and knew it," so the meaning becomes: "so we believed in it, that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord..." Al-Farra' preceded him in a similar view, saying: "(anna) is read with fatha because belief falls upon it. You will find that belief is fitting in some of what is read with fatha and not in others, but that does not prevent you from keeping them all with fatha, for what necessitates fatha of (anna) fits there, such as (we affirmed) and (we testified)."

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 72, verses 1–15 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Farra' pointed out that some of what has been given the fatha does not fit with governing "āmannā" over it, such as His saying: ﴿And that we thought that mankind and the jinn would never speak a lie against God﴾. Al-Zamakhshari followed them both and said: "As for whoever gave all of them the fatha, it is by way of conjunction with the place of the prepositional phrase in ﴿we believed in it﴾, as if it were said: 'We affirmed it, and we affirmed that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, and that he [i.e., the foolish one among us] used to say...' and likewise the rest." End of quote. He did not perceive what al-Farra' perceived, namely that some of them cannot properly be governed by (āmannā).

The majority read ﴿jadd rabbinā﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a damma on the dal, in construct with "rabbinā," meaning: His majesty (ʿaẓamatuhu). This is the view of the majority. Anas and al-Hasan said: His wealth/sufficiency (ghināhu). Mujahid said: His mention (dhikruhu). Ibn ʿAbbas said: His rank and His command (qadruhu wa amruhu). ʿIkrima read (jaddun) with tanwin, (rabbunā) in the nominative, as if he said: "He is great, our Lord," so "rabbunā" is a substitute (badal). Al-jadd in the language means "the great." Humayd ibn Qays read jaddun with a damma on the jim, in construct, and its meaning is "the great," transmitted by Sibawayh; it is an idafa of the attribute to the thing described, and the meaning is: "Exalted is our Lord, the Great." ʿIkrima also read jaddan rabbunā, with fatha on the jim and dal, tanwin, and raising of "rabbunā," with jaddan in the accusative as a tamyiz transferred from the subject; its origin is "Exalted is the majesty of our Lord." Qatada and ʿIkrima also read jiddan with kasra on the jim and tanwin, in the accusative, with "rabbunā" raised. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: jiddan is accusative as a ḥāl, and its meaning is: "exalted in truth and in power." Others said: it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, its estimate being: "ta'ālayā jiddan," and rabbunā is nominative by taʿālā. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ read jaddayi rabbinā, meaning: His bounty and benefit. The majority read ﴿yaqūlu safīhunā﴾: it is Iblis. It was also said: it is a collective noun for every fool, and Iblis is the leader of the fools. Al-shatat means transgression and going beyond the due measure. Al-A'sha said:
Will they desist, when he will not forbid those of excess, / like a spear-thrust from which oil and wick flow out.
It is said: "ashatta fi al-sawm" when one goes far in the bargain, meaning: a statement which is in itself excess, which is the attribution of a consort and a son to God, exalted is He.

﴿And that we thought﴾ the verse: that is, we had thought well of mankind and the jinn, and we believed that no one would dare to lie against God by attributing to Him a consort and a son. So we believed in the truth of what Iblis and his rebels had led us astray with, until we heard the Qur'an and clarified their lie.

The majority read ﴿an lan taqūla﴾, the imperfect of qāla. Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra, Yaʿqub, and Ibn Miqsam read taqawwala, the imperfect of tataqawwalu, with one of the two tas omitted. In the majority reading, "kadhiban" is accusative by "taqūla," because a lie is a kind of speech, or it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: "a speech, a lie," i.e., a fabricated speech. In the anomalous reading it is a verbal noun of "taqūla," since it is itself lying, so it is like "qa'adtu juluusan" (I sat sitting).

﴿And that there were men﴾. The majority narrated that a man, when he wished to spend the night or settle in a valley, would call out at the top of his voice: "O Master of this valley! I seek refuge in you from the foolish ones who are in your obedience," believing that the jinni in the valley would protect and shield him. It is reported that the jinn would then say: "We possess neither for you nor for ourselves anything from God." Muqatil said: The first people to seek refuge with the jinn were a people from Yemen, then the Banu Hanifa, then this spread among the Arabs. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun subject in (fa-zādūhum) refers to ﴿men from mankind﴾, since they are the ones spoken of; this is the view of Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr. (fa-zādūhum): that is, mankind increased them (rahaqan): that is, audacity, arrogance, insolence, transgression, and committing what is forbidden, and self-admiration, to the extent that they said: "We have mastered mankind and the jinn." Some explained rahaq as sin. Al-Tabari cited the verse of al-A'sha on this:
Nothing benefits me apart from seeing her; / the lover is not healed unless he has been struck with rahaq.
He said its meaning: "unless he has committed the forbidden." The meaning is: mankind increased the jinn in sin, because they glorified them, so they increased them in permitting themselves the prohibitions of God, exalted is He. Qatada, Abu al-ʿAliya, al-Rabiʿ, and Ibn Zayd said: (fa-zādūhum): that is, the jinn increased mankind in fear, imagining to them to the utmost of their ability, and misleading them, since they saw the lightness of their judgment, so they despised and belittled them. Ibn Jubayr said: (rahaqan) means disbelief. It was also said: the word "rijāl" is not applied to the jinn, so the meaning is: "And there were men from mankind who sought refuge from the evil of the jinn with men from mankind," and a man would say, for example: "I seek refuge with Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman from the jinn of this valley." This is a strange view.

(And that they) that is, the disbelievers of mankind ﴿thought as you thought﴾, O jinn, addressing one another. Both "thought" and "you thought" each require ﴿that God would not raise up﴾, so the matter is one of tanāzuʿ (operating on a common complement), and "an" here is the lightened form of the heavy "anna." It was also said: the pronoun in (and that they) refers to the jinn, and the address in "you thought" is to Quraysh, and this and the one before it are from what is revealed, not from the speech of the jinn: ﴿that God would never raise up anyone﴾: the apparent meaning is the sending of a messenger to creation, and this is most fitting to what precedes and follows the verses. It was also said: the resurrection.

﴿And that we touched the heaven﴾: the original meaning of lams is touch; then it was used figuratively for seeking, and the meaning is: we sought to reach the heaven in order to listen to the speech of its inhabitants, and we found it filled. The apparent meaning is that "wajada" here means "encountered and found," and it took one object, and the clause "mulli'at" is in the position of a ḥāl. It was also permitted that it take two objects, with (fa-mulli'at) in the position of the second object. al-A'raj read mulīyat with ya without hamza; the majority read with hamza. And shadīdan is an attribute of al-ḥaras according to the wording, because it is a collective noun, as he said:
I fear a little rujayl or a little rukayb, a hostile one.
Were the meaning observed, he would say shiddādan in the plural. The apparent meaning of al-ḥaras is the angels, that is, guarding against the devils approaching it, and shuhuban is the plural of shihab, which is what the devils are pelted with when they listen. It was said: it is possible that the shuhub are the ḥaras; the meaning is repeated when the wording differs, as in:
And Hind—between her and me there came distance and remoteness.
His saying: ﴿we found it filled﴾ indicates that previously they used to sneak into the heaven and did not find it filled. (maqā'id) is the plural of maq'ad, and the Messenger of God ﷺ explained the form of the jinn's sitting: "They were one above another, and whenever the upper one was burned, the one beneath him rose into his place. They would steal a word and throw it to the soothsayers, adding to it, and then the soothsayers would add to the word a hundred lies."

﴿Now whoever listens﴾: "al-ān" is a time adverb for the present, and "yastamiʿu" is in the future; the adverb was stretched and used for the future, as he said:
I will strive now, when its limit is reached.
The meaning is: whoever among them listens in the coming time ﴿will find for himself a watching flame﴾, that is, one who watches for him and burns him. This is for whoever listens. As for hearing, it has ceased, as God said: ﴿Indeed they are cut off from hearing﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 212]. The stoning was in the Jahiliyya, and that is mentioned in their poetry, and the hadith indicates it when he, peace be upon him, saw a star that had been shot down, and said: "What did you used to say about such a thing in the Jahiliyya?" They said: "We used to say: a great one dies or a great one is born." Aws ibn Hajar said:
It leapt like a pearl, followed by / a dust cloud rising, you would think it a tent-rope.
ʿAwf ibn al-Jaz' said:
So he returned to us the caravan, apart from its mate, / or the bull like a pearl, followed by blood.
Bishr ibn Abi Hazim said:
The caravan is overtaken by dust, and its foal / darts after the two like the darting of a star.
Al-Tibrizi said: all these poets are Jahiliyya; there is none among them who was a mukhadram. Ma'mar said: I said to al-Zuhri: "Were stars shot at in the Jahiliyya?" He said: "Yes." I said: "What do you say about His saying: ﴿and that we used to sit in it in places for listening﴾?" He said: "Its matter was made severe and intensified when the Messenger of God was sent." Al-Jahiz said: the view that it was shooting is more correct, because of His saying: ﴿we found it filled﴾, and this is information from the jinn that the guard of the heaven was increased until it was filled, and because of what Ibn ʿAbbas narrated, and he mentioned the earlier hadith. Al-Zamakhshari, following al-Jahiz, said: in His saying is proof that the ḥaras is fullness and abundance, therefore ﴿we used to sit in it in places﴾, that is, we used to find some of the places empty of guards and meteors, and now all the places are filled. End of quote. All of this refutes the view of those who say that the stoning occurred after the mission of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and that it was one of his signs. The apparent meaning of "rasadan" is: "possessors of a meteor, watching with the stoning," and they are the angels who pelt them with shooting stars and prevent them from listening.

When they saw what had happened of the great stoning and the prevention of eavesdropping, they said: ﴿We do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth﴾, which is their disbelief in this Prophet ﷺ, so that evil would befall them, ﴿or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance﴾, so that they would believe in him and be guided. When they mentioned evil, they did not attribute it to God, exalted is He; when they mentioned guidance, they attributed it to Him, exalted is He.

﴿And that among us are the righteous﴾: they informed of what they were upon of righteousness and otherwise.

﴿And among us are those below that﴾: that is, below the righteous. "Dūna" occurs in places where "ghayr" would occur, so it is as if he said: "and among us are non-righteous." It is also permitted that they meant: "and among us are those below that in righteousness," that is, among them are the pious, and among them are those who are not complete in righteousness. "Dūna" is in the position of an attribute of an omitted noun, meaning: "and among us are a people below that." This omitted described noun may be dropped in the division with "min," even in clauses; they say: "Among us are those who departed, and among us are those who stayed," meaning: "among us is a group that departed, and among us is a group that stayed." The clause ﴿we were paths, separate groups﴾ is an explanation of the earlier division. Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, and Qatada said: divergent desires; it was also said: divergent sects. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, we were people of divergent ways, or we were in our divergent conditions like divergent paths, or we were on divergent paths, as in His saying: "as the fox made the path [smooth]," or our paths were qidad, with the omission of the mudaf which is "paths" and the mudaf ilayhi (the pronoun) standing in its place. End of quote. In his first two estimates, the omission is of the mudaf from "paths" and the mudaf ilayhi standing in its place, since he omitted "possessors of" and "like." As for the third estimate, that it be accusative by dropping "fi" (in), this is not permitted except in necessity, and Sibawayh explicitly stated that ʿasala al-ṭarīq is anomalous, so the Qur'an is not to be construed upon it.

﴿And that we thought that we would not frustrate God﴾: that is, we were certain ﴿in the earth﴾: that is, existing in the earth ﴿and we would not frustrate Him by flight﴾: that is, from the earth to the heaven. "Fi al-ard" and "haraban" are two ḥāls, that is, fleeing or fugitives.

﴿And that when we heard the guidance﴾: which is the Qur'an ﴿we believed in it﴾: that is, in the Qur'an ﴿so whoever believes in his Lord will not fear﴾: that is, he does not fear. Ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, and the majority read ﴿fa-lā yakhāfu﴾, and their reading is taken as a negation. It was also said: the fa' is extra and there is no negation. This is not correct. The answer with fa' was better than bringing the verb in the jussive without fa', because when it is with fa' it is by way of an implied subject, that is: "so he does not fear." The nominal clause is more indicative and more emphatic than the verbal clause in establishing the content of the clause. (bakhsan) Ibn ʿAbbas said: the diminishing of good deeds; ﴿nor any injustice﴾ he said: an increase in bad deeds; ﴿nor any injustice﴾ it was said: the imposition of what cannot be borne. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, a recompense of diminution or injustice; because he diminishes no one's right and does not commit injustice against anyone, so he does not fear the recompense of either. It is also permitted that it be meant: "so he does not fear that he will be diminished, but he will be rewarded with the fullest reward, nor that disgrace will overtake him," from His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿disgrace will overtake them﴾ [al-Qalam: 43]. End of quote.

The majority read (bakhsan) with sukun on the kha'. Ibn Thabit read it with fatha.

﴿And among us are the qasitun﴾: that is, the disbelievers who deviate from the truth. Mujahid and Qatada said: "qasit" is the wrongdoer, the unjust; and from this is the verse of the poet:

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 72, verses 1–15 (part 3 of 3)**

A verse of poetry:

*"A people who killed the son of Hind by force,*
*and who were unjust to al-Nu'man."*

This division came, although it had already been mentioned in ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that﴾, to mention the condition of the two groups, those who are saved and those who are destroyed, and to encourage whoever enters Islam. The apparent meaning is that ﴿Whoever submits﴾ up to the end of the two conditions is part of the speech of the jinn. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The better view is that ﴿Whoever submits﴾ is an address from God Most High to Muhammad (ﷺ), and the verses that follow support this."

al-A'raj recited *rushdan* (رُشْدًا) with a *damma* on the *ra'* and a *sukun* on the *shin*. The majority recite it with a *fatha* on both. al-Zamakhshari said: "Someone who does not hold that the jinn receive reward has claimed that God Most High threatened their unjust ones but did not promise reward to their Muslims, and that is threat enough." That is, *fa-ulā'ika taharraw rashadan* (فَأُولَئِكَ تَحَرَّوْا رَشَدًا), so he mentioned the cause of the reward and what makes it due, and God is too just to punish the unjust while not rewarding the rightly guided. End of quotation. In it there is a hidden insinuation (*dasisah*) of Mu'tazilism (the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, a rationalist theological school) in his phrase "and what makes it due."

[p. 344]

**Surat al-Jinn is Meccan and has twenty-eight verses.**

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened and said: "We have heard a wondrous Qur'an,﴾ ﴿guiding to right conduct, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord.﴾ ﴿And that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, has taken neither a consort nor a son.﴾ ﴿And that our foolish one used to speak against God with outrageous falsehood.﴾ ﴿And that we had thought that humans and jinn would never tell lies about God.﴾ ﴿And that some men of mankind used to seek refuge with some men of the jinn, so they increased them in distress.﴾ ﴿And that they thought, as you thought, that God would never raise anyone up.﴾ ﴿And that we touched the heaven and found it filled with severe guards and meteors.﴾ ﴿And that we used to sit in some of its places to listen, but whoever listens now finds a watching meteor lying in wait for him.﴾ ﴿And that we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance.﴾ ﴿And that among us are the righteous, and among us are others below that; we were of divers ways.﴾ ﴿And that we thought we could not escape God on earth, nor could we escape Him by flight.﴾ ﴿And that when we heard the guidance, we believed in it; so whoever believes in his Lord fears neither loss nor distress.﴾ ﴿And that among us are the Muslims, and among us are the deviators. Whoever submits, those have sought out right guidance.﴾ ﴿But as for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell.﴾ ﴿And that if they had remained upright on the path, We would have given them abundant water to drink.﴾ ﴿That We might test them therein. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And that the mosques belong to God, so do not call upon anyone along with God.﴾ ﴿And that when the servant of God stood calling upon Him, they nearly became a crowd pressing upon him.﴾ ﴿Say: I only call upon my Lord and I associate no one with Him.﴾ ﴿Say: I do not control for you any harm or any right guidance.﴾ ﴿Say: No one can protect me from God, nor will I find any refuge besides Him.﴾ ﴿Except a message from God and His messages. And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever.﴾ ﴿Until, when they see what they are promised, they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number.﴾ ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will appoint for it a long term.﴾ ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone,﴾ ﴿except a messenger whom He has chosen; for indeed He sends before him and behind him a guard,﴾ ﴿that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord. And He encompasses what is with them and has counted everything in number.﴾

[p. 345]

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened and said: "We have heard a wondrous Qur'an,﴾ ... ﴿and as for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell.﴾

[p. 346]

This surah is Meccan. Its connection with what precedes it is this: when God related the persistence of the people of Noah in disbelief and their devotion to idol worship, and Noah (peace be upon him) was the first messenger to the earth, just as Muhammad (ﷺ) is the last messenger to the earth, and the Arabs, of whom he (peace be upon him) was one, were worshippers of idols like the people of Noah, to the point that they worshipped idols similar to those in name, and what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought of the Qur'an was a guide to right conduct, and the Arabs had heard it, yet most of them hesitated to believe in it, God revealed Surat al-Jinn immediately after Surat Nuh, as a rebuke to the Quraysh and the Arabs for their slowness to believe, since the jinn were better than them and more receptive to belief, even though they were not of the same kind as the Messenger (ﷺ). Yet by merely hearing the Qur'an, they were overawed by it and believed in it at once, and they knew that it was not of the pattern of human speech. By contrast, the Arabs, although it was revealed in their tongue and they recognised that it was inimitable, denied it and those who brought it out of envy and insolence, that God should send down His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read ﴿qul uhiya﴾ with four radicals (uhiya, passive of aha). Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Ataki, from Abu Amr, and Abu Unas Juwayya ibn A'idh al-Asadi read (wuhiya) with three radicals. It is said: waha and awha have the same meaning. Al-Ajjaj said:

*He drew to her the settled ground, and she settled.*

Zayd ibn Ali and Juwayya, as transmitted from al-Kisa'i and Ibn Abi Ablah also, read (uhiya) by replacing the waw with a hamza, just as they said in (wa'ada) (he promised): (a'ada). Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is from the unrestricted interchange (al-qalb al-mutlaq), whose permissibility applies to every waw that is pronounced with damma." End of quotation. It is not as he mentioned; rather, there is detail here, namely that the waw with damma may occur initially, medially, or finally, and each has its own rules, and some of these are disputed and detailed in grammar. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-Mazini applied this even to the kasra, as in (ishah) and (isadah) and (i'a akhihi)." End of quotation. This is exaggeration and showing off. He used to mention this in ﴿wi'a akhihi﴾ [Yusuf 76] in the surah of Yusuf. Al-Mazini had two opinions on this: one, that it is by analogy as he said; the other, that it is restricted to what is heard (samā').

The phrase ﴿annahu istama'a﴾ is in the position of the object of the passive verb, i.e., the listening (istima') of "a company of the jinn." The well-known view is that this listening is the one mentioned in al-Ahqaf in God's words: ﴿And when We turned towards you a company of the jinn who listened to the Qur'an﴾ [al-Ahqaf 29], and it is one single incident. It is also said there were two incidents: the jinn who came to him in Mecca were the jinn of Nasibin, and those who came to him at Nakhla were the jinn of Nineveh. As for the surah they heard, Ikrima said it was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-Alaq 1]. It was also said it was Surat al-Rahman. The verse does not address, neither here nor in al-Ahqaf, whether he saw them and spoke to them (peace be upon him). What appears from the hadith is that it happened twice. The first was at the beginning of the prophetic mission of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), at the time when Abdullah ibn Mas'ud reported that he was not with him on the night of the jinn. They had lost him (peace be upon him), and they searched for him in the valleys and ravines but did not find him. When morning came, behold, he came from the direction of Hira. In it: "The caller of the jinn came to me, so I went with him (p. 347) and recited the Qur'an to them. He set out with us and showed us their traces and the traces of their fires." The second time, Ibn Mas'ud was with him. The Prophet (ﷺ) had called upon anyone to accompany him to recite the Qur'an to the jinn, but no one rose except Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. He went with him to al-Hajun near the ravine. He drew a line for him and said: "Do not cross it." Then there descended upon him (peace be upon him) like stones, they dragged the stones with their feet, walking and beating their drums as women beat their tambourines, until they covered him, and I could no longer see him, so I stood up. He signalled to me with his hand to sit. He recited the Qur'an, and his voice kept rising, and they vanished into the earth until I could no longer see them." The hadith. That these were two incidents is shown by their disagreement about the number: it was said seven, and it was said nine. From Zirr: they were three from the people of Harran and four from the people of Nasibin, a town in Yemen other than the town in Iraq. From Ikrima: they were twelve thousand from the island of Mosul. And where are seven out of twelve thousand?

﴿So they said: "We have heard a wondrous Qur'an"﴾. That is, they said to their people when they returned to them, and they described (Qur'anan) by saying (ajaban), describing it with the verbal noun as an intensification, meaning: it is wondrous in itself, for the eloquence of its speech, the goodness of its structures, the subtlety of its meanings, the strangeness of its style, the eloquence of its admonitions, and its being unlike all other books. And 'ajab (wonder) is what departs from any of its forms and analogues.

﴿Guiding to right conduct﴾: that is, it calls to what is correct. It is also said: to monotheism and faith. Al-Jumhur read (al-rushd) with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the shin. Isa read both with damma. Also from him: both with fatha.

﴿So we have believed in it﴾: that is, in the Qur'an. Since belief in it includes belief in God and in His oneness and freedom from polytheism, they said: ﴿and we will never associate anyone with our Lord﴾. The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi', of Mecca and Medina) and the two Abus read with fatha the hamza in His words ﴿wa-annahu ta'ala﴾ and what follows it, twelve verses, the last of which is ﴿wa-anna minna al-muslimun﴾. The remaining seven read with kasra. As for the kasra, it is clear, because these are conjoined to His words ﴿inna sami'na﴾, so they are included within the object of the saying. As for the fatha, Abu Hatim said: it is governed by (uhiya), so all of it is in the position of nominative as the object not named as agent. End of quotation. This is not correct, because among the conjoined elements is that which cannot be included under (uhiya), namely whatever contains the first-person pronoun, as in His words: ﴿And that we used to sit in some of its places to listen﴾. Do you not see that it does not fit with ﴿It has been revealed to me﴾ followed by ﴿that we used to sit in some of its places﴾? And the same applies to the rest. The reading with fatha is explained as follows: all these are conjoined to the pronoun governed by the preposition in (bihi) in His words ﴿so we have believed in it﴾, meaning "and [we believed] that He..." and so on for the rest. This is permissible according to the Kufans' view, and it is the correct view. We have already argued for the validity of this in His words ﴿and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah 217]. Makki said: it is better in that the omission of the preposition before (anna) is more frequent in the rest. Al-Zajjaj said: its explanation is that it is treated as governed by (amanna bihi), because its meaning is: "we accepted it and knew it," so the meaning becomes: "so we believed in it, that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord..." Al-Farra' preceded him in a similar view, saying: "(anna) is read with fatha because belief falls upon it. You will find that belief is fitting in some of what is read with fatha and not in others, but that does not prevent you from keeping them all with fatha, for what necessitates fatha of (anna) fits there, such as (we affirmed) and (we testified)."

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 72, verses 1–15 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Farra' pointed out that some of what has been given the fatha does not fit with governing "āmannā" over it, such as His saying: ﴿And that we thought that mankind and the jinn would never speak a lie against God﴾. Al-Zamakhshari followed them both and said: "As for whoever gave all of them the fatha, it is by way of conjunction with the place of the prepositional phrase in ﴿we believed in it﴾, as if it were said: 'We affirmed it, and we affirmed that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, and that he [i.e., the foolish one among us] used to say...' and likewise the rest." End of quote. He did not perceive what al-Farra' perceived, namely that some of them cannot properly be governed by (āmannā).

The majority read ﴿jadd rabbinā﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a damma on the dal, in construct with "rabbinā," meaning: His majesty (ʿaẓamatuhu). This is the view of the majority. Anas and al-Hasan said: His wealth/sufficiency (ghināhu). Mujahid said: His mention (dhikruhu). Ibn ʿAbbas said: His rank and His command (qadruhu wa amruhu). ʿIkrima read (jaddun) with tanwin, (rabbunā) in the nominative, as if he said: "He is great, our Lord," so "rabbunā" is a substitute (badal). Al-jadd in the language means "the great." Humayd ibn Qays read jaddun with a damma on the jim, in construct, and its meaning is "the great," transmitted by Sibawayh; it is an idafa of the attribute to the thing described, and the meaning is: "Exalted is our Lord, the Great." ʿIkrima also read jaddan rabbunā, with fatha on the jim and dal, tanwin, and raising of "rabbunā," with jaddan in the accusative as a tamyiz transferred from the subject; its origin is "Exalted is the majesty of our Lord." Qatada and ʿIkrima also read jiddan with kasra on the jim and tanwin, in the accusative, with "rabbunā" raised. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: jiddan is accusative as a ḥāl, and its meaning is: "exalted in truth and in power." Others said: it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, its estimate being: "ta'ālayā jiddan," and rabbunā is nominative by taʿālā. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ read jaddayi rabbinā, meaning: His bounty and benefit. The majority read ﴿yaqūlu safīhunā﴾: it is Iblis. It was also said: it is a collective noun for every fool, and Iblis is the leader of the fools. Al-shatat means transgression and going beyond the due measure. Al-A'sha said:
Will they desist, when he will not forbid those of excess, / like a spear-thrust from which oil and wick flow out.
It is said: "ashatta fi al-sawm" when one goes far in the bargain, meaning: a statement which is in itself excess, which is the attribution of a consort and a son to God, exalted is He.

﴿And that we thought﴾ the verse: that is, we had thought well of mankind and the jinn, and we believed that no one would dare to lie against God by attributing to Him a consort and a son. So we believed in the truth of what Iblis and his rebels had led us astray with, until we heard the Qur'an and clarified their lie.

The majority read ﴿an lan taqūla﴾, the imperfect of qāla. Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra, Yaʿqub, and Ibn Miqsam read taqawwala, the imperfect of tataqawwalu, with one of the two tas omitted. In the majority reading, "kadhiban" is accusative by "taqūla," because a lie is a kind of speech, or it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: "a speech, a lie," i.e., a fabricated speech. In the anomalous reading it is a verbal noun of "taqūla," since it is itself lying, so it is like "qa'adtu juluusan" (I sat sitting).

﴿And that there were men﴾. The majority narrated that a man, when he wished to spend the night or settle in a valley, would call out at the top of his voice: "O Master of this valley! I seek refuge in you from the foolish ones who are in your obedience," believing that the jinni in the valley would protect and shield him. It is reported that the jinn would then say: "We possess neither for you nor for ourselves anything from God." Muqatil said: The first people to seek refuge with the jinn were a people from Yemen, then the Banu Hanifa, then this spread among the Arabs. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun subject in (fa-zādūhum) refers to ﴿men from mankind﴾, since they are the ones spoken of; this is the view of Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr. (fa-zādūhum): that is, mankind increased them (rahaqan): that is, audacity, arrogance, insolence, transgression, and committing what is forbidden, and self-admiration, to the extent that they said: "We have mastered mankind and the jinn." Some explained rahaq as sin. Al-Tabari cited the verse of al-A'sha on this:
Nothing benefits me apart from seeing her; / the lover is not healed unless he has been struck with rahaq.
He said its meaning: "unless he has committed the forbidden." The meaning is: mankind increased the jinn in sin, because they glorified them, so they increased them in permitting themselves the prohibitions of God, exalted is He. Qatada, Abu al-ʿAliya, al-Rabiʿ, and Ibn Zayd said: (fa-zādūhum): that is, the jinn increased mankind in fear, imagining to them to the utmost of their ability, and misleading them, since they saw the lightness of their judgment, so they despised and belittled them. Ibn Jubayr said: (rahaqan) means disbelief. It was also said: the word "rijāl" is not applied to the jinn, so the meaning is: "And there were men from mankind who sought refuge from the evil of the jinn with men from mankind," and a man would say, for example: "I seek refuge with Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman from the jinn of this valley." This is a strange view.

(And that they) that is, the disbelievers of mankind ﴿thought as you thought﴾, O jinn, addressing one another. Both "thought" and "you thought" each require ﴿that God would not raise up﴾, so the matter is one of tanāzuʿ (operating on a common complement), and "an" here is the lightened form of the heavy "anna." It was also said: the pronoun in (and that they) refers to the jinn, and the address in "you thought" is to Quraysh, and this and the one before it are from what is revealed, not from the speech of the jinn: ﴿that God would never raise up anyone﴾: the apparent meaning is the sending of a messenger to creation, and this is most fitting to what precedes and follows the verses. It was also said: the resurrection.

﴿And that we touched the heaven﴾: the original meaning of lams is touch; then it was used figuratively for seeking, and the meaning is: we sought to reach the heaven in order to listen to the speech of its inhabitants, and we found it filled. The apparent meaning is that "wajada" here means "encountered and found," and it took one object, and the clause "mulli'at" is in the position of a ḥāl. It was also permitted that it take two objects, with (fa-mulli'at) in the position of the second object. al-A'raj read mulīyat with ya without hamza; the majority read with hamza. And shadīdan is an attribute of al-ḥaras according to the wording, because it is a collective noun, as he said:
I fear a little rujayl or a little rukayb, a hostile one.
Were the meaning observed, he would say shiddādan in the plural. The apparent meaning of al-ḥaras is the angels, that is, guarding against the devils approaching it, and shuhuban is the plural of shihab, which is what the devils are pelted with when they listen. It was said: it is possible that the shuhub are the ḥaras; the meaning is repeated when the wording differs, as in:
And Hind—between her and me there came distance and remoteness.
His saying: ﴿we found it filled﴾ indicates that previously they used to sneak into the heaven and did not find it filled. (maqā'id) is the plural of maq'ad, and the Messenger of God ﷺ explained the form of the jinn's sitting: "They were one above another, and whenever the upper one was burned, the one beneath him rose into his place. They would steal a word and throw it to the soothsayers, adding to it, and then the soothsayers would add to the word a hundred lies."

﴿Now whoever listens﴾: "al-ān" is a time adverb for the present, and "yastamiʿu" is in the future; the adverb was stretched and used for the future, as he said:
I will strive now, when its limit is reached.
The meaning is: whoever among them listens in the coming time ﴿will find for himself a watching flame﴾, that is, one who watches for him and burns him. This is for whoever listens. As for hearing, it has ceased, as God said: ﴿Indeed they are cut off from hearing﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 212].
