It was also permitted that it take two objects, with (fa-mulli'at) in the position of the second object. al-A'raj read mulīyat with ya without hamza; the majority read with hamza. And shadīdan is an attribute of al-ḥaras according to the wording, because it is a collective noun, as he said:
I fear a little rujayl or a little rukayb, a hostile one.
Were the meaning observed, he would say shiddādan in the plural. The apparent meaning of al-ḥaras is the angels, that is, guarding against the devils approaching it, and shuhuban is the plural of shihab, which is what the devils are pelted with when they listen. It was said: it is possible that the shuhub are the ḥaras; the meaning is repeated when the wording differs, as in:
And Hind—between her and me there came distance and remoteness.
His saying: ﴿we found it filled﴾ indicates that previously they used to sneak into the heaven and did not find it filled. (maqā'id) is the plural of maq'ad, and the Messenger of God ﷺ explained the form of the jinn's sitting: "They were one above another, and whenever the upper one was burned, the one beneath him rose into his place. They would steal a word and throw it to the soothsayers, adding to it, and then the soothsayers would add to the word a hundred lies."

﴿Now whoever listens﴾: "al-ān" is a time adverb for the present, and "yastamiʿu" is in the future; the adverb was stretched and used for the future, as he said:
I will strive now, when its limit is reached.
The meaning is: whoever among them listens in the coming time ﴿will find for himself a watching flame﴾, that is, one who watches for him and burns him. This is for whoever listens. As for hearing, it has ceased, as God said: ﴿Indeed they are cut off from hearing﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 212]. The stoning was in the Jahiliyya, and that is mentioned in their poetry, and the hadith indicates it when he, peace be upon him, saw a star that had been shot down, and said: "What did you used to say about such a thing in the Jahiliyya?" They said: "We used to say: a great one dies or a great one is born." Aws ibn Hajar said:
It leapt like a pearl, followed by / a dust cloud rising, you would think it a tent-rope.
ʿAwf ibn al-Jaz' said:
So he returned to us the caravan, apart from its mate, / or the bull like a pearl, followed by blood.
Bishr ibn Abi Hazim said:
The caravan is overtaken by dust, and its foal / darts after the two like the darting of a star.
Al-Tibrizi said: all these poets are Jahiliyya; there is none among them who was a mukhadram. Ma'mar said: I said to al-Zuhri: "Were stars shot at in the Jahiliyya?" He said: "Yes." I said: "What do you say about His saying: ﴿and that we used to sit in it in places for listening﴾?" He said: "Its matter was made severe and intensified when the Messenger of God was sent." Al-Jahiz said: the view that it was shooting is more correct, because of His saying: ﴿we found it filled﴾, and this is information from the jinn that the guard of the heaven was increased until it was filled, and because of what Ibn ʿAbbas narrated, and he mentioned the earlier hadith. Al-Zamakhshari, following al-Jahiz, said: in His saying is proof that the ḥaras is fullness and abundance, therefore ﴿we used to sit in it in places﴾, that is, we used to find some of the places empty of guards and meteors, and now all the places are filled. End of quote. All of this refutes the view of those who say that the stoning occurred after the mission of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and that it was one of his signs. The apparent meaning of "rasadan" is: "possessors of a meteor, watching with the stoning," and they are the angels who pelt them with shooting stars and prevent them from listening.

When they saw what had happened of the great stoning and the prevention of eavesdropping, they said: ﴿We do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth﴾, which is their disbelief in this Prophet ﷺ, so that evil would befall them, ﴿or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance﴾, so that they would believe in him and be guided. When they mentioned evil, they did not attribute it to God, exalted is He; when they mentioned guidance, they attributed it to Him, exalted is He.

﴿And that among us are the righteous﴾: they informed of what they were upon of righteousness and otherwise.

﴿And among us are those below that﴾: that is, below the righteous. "Dūna" occurs in places where "ghayr" would occur, so it is as if he said: "and among us are non-righteous." It is also permitted that they meant: "and among us are those below that in righteousness," that is, among them are the pious, and among them are those who are not complete in righteousness. "Dūna" is in the position of an attribute of an omitted noun, meaning: "and among us are a people below that." This omitted described noun may be dropped in the division with "min," even in clauses; they say: "Among us are those who departed, and among us are those who stayed," meaning: "among us is a group that departed, and among us is a group that stayed." The clause ﴿we were paths, separate groups﴾ is an explanation of the earlier division. Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, and Qatada said: divergent desires; it was also said: divergent sects. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, we were people of divergent ways, or we were in our divergent conditions like divergent paths, or we were on divergent paths, as in His saying: "as the fox made the path [smooth]," or our paths were qidad, with the omission of the mudaf which is "paths" and the mudaf ilayhi (the pronoun) standing in its place. End of quote. In his first two estimates, the omission is of the mudaf from "paths" and the mudaf ilayhi standing in its place, since he omitted "possessors of" and "like." As for the third estimate, that it be accusative by dropping "fi" (in), this is not permitted except in necessity, and Sibawayh explicitly stated that ʿasala al-ṭarīq is anomalous, so the Qur'an is not to be construed upon it.

﴿And that we thought that we would not frustrate God﴾: that is, we were certain ﴿in the earth﴾: that is, existing in the earth ﴿and we would not frustrate Him by flight﴾: that is, from the earth to the heaven. "Fi al-ard" and "haraban" are two ḥāls, that is, fleeing or fugitives.

﴿And that when we heard the guidance﴾: which is the Qur'an ﴿we believed in it﴾: that is, in the Qur'an ﴿so whoever believes in his Lord will not fear﴾: that is, he does not fear. Ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, and the majority read ﴿fa-lā yakhāfu﴾, and their reading is taken as a negation. It was also said: the fa' is extra and there is no negation. This is not correct. The answer with fa' was better than bringing the verb in the jussive without fa', because when it is with fa' it is by way of an implied subject, that is: "so he does not fear." The nominal clause is more indicative and more emphatic than the verbal clause in establishing the content of the clause. (bakhsan) Ibn ʿAbbas said: the diminishing of good deeds; ﴿nor any injustice﴾ he said: an increase in bad deeds; ﴿nor any injustice﴾ it was said: the imposition of what cannot be borne. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, a recompense of diminution or injustice; because he diminishes no one's right and does not commit injustice against anyone, so he does not fear the recompense of either. It is also permitted that it be meant: "so he does not fear that he will be diminished, but he will be rewarded with the fullest reward, nor that disgrace will overtake him," from His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿disgrace will overtake them﴾ [al-Qalam: 43]. End of quote.

The majority read (bakhsan) with sukun on the kha'. Ibn Thabit read it with fatha.

﴿And among us are the qasitun﴾: that is, the disbelievers who deviate from the truth. Mujahid and Qatada said: "qasit" is the wrongdoer, the unjust; and from this is the verse of the poet:

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 72, verses 1–15 (part 3 of 3)**

A verse of poetry:

*"A people who killed the son of Hind by force,*
*and who were unjust to al-Nu'man."*

This division came, although it had already been mentioned in ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that﴾, to mention the condition of the two groups, those who are saved and those who are destroyed, and to encourage whoever enters Islam. The apparent meaning is that ﴿Whoever submits﴾ up to the end of the two conditions is part of the speech of the jinn. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The better view is that ﴿Whoever submits﴾ is an address from God Most High to Muhammad (ﷺ), and the verses that follow support this."

al-A'raj recited *rushdan* (رُشْدًا) with a *damma* on the *ra'* and a *sukun* on the *shin*. The majority recite it with a *fatha* on both. al-Zamakhshari said: "Someone who does not hold that the jinn receive reward has claimed that God Most High threatened their unjust ones but did not promise reward to their Muslims, and that is threat enough." That is, *fa-ulā'ika taharraw rashadan* (فَأُولَئِكَ تَحَرَّوْا رَشَدًا), so he mentioned the cause of the reward and what makes it due, and God is too just to punish the unjust while not rewarding the rightly guided. End of quotation. In it there is a hidden insinuation (*dasisah*) of Mu'tazilism (the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, a rationalist theological school) in his phrase "and what makes it due."

﴿And that if they had remained upright on the path, We would have given them abundant water﴾ [al-Jinn: 16]. ﴿So that We might test them therein. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a severe punishment﴾ [al-Jinn: 17]. ﴿And that the mosques belong to Allah, so do not invoke anyone alongside Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18]. ﴿And that when the servant of Allah stood calling upon Him, they almost became a crowd pressing upon him﴾ [al-Jinn: 19]. ﴿Say: "I only invoke my Lord and associate no one with Him"﴾ [al-Jinn: 20]. ﴿Say: "I do not possess for you any harm or any right guidance"﴾ [al-Jinn: 21]. ﴿Say: "No one can protect me from Allah, nor will I find any refuge besides Him"﴾ [al-Jinn: 22], ﴿except a conveyance from Allah and His messages. And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, indeed, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn: 23]. ﴿Until, when they see what they are promised, they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number﴾ [al-Jinn: 24]. ﴿Say: "I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will set for it a long term"﴾ [al-Jinn: 25]. ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone﴾ [al-Jinn: 26], ﴿except one whom He has approved of among messengers; indeed, He sends before him and behind him guards﴾ [al-Jinn: 27], ﴿so that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord. And He has encompassed what is with them and has enumerated everything in number﴾ [al-Jinn: 28].

This is part of what is revealed under ﴿It has been revealed to me﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]. The word ﴿أنْ﴾ (an) is the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy ﴿inna﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَقامُوا﴾ (istaqamu, "they remained upright") refers to the following. Al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Zayd ibn Aslam and Abu Mijlaz said: it refers to the words ﴿فَمَن أسْلَمَ﴾ (fa-man aslama, "whoever submits") [al-Jinn: 14], and "the path" (al-tariqa) is the path of disbelief; that is, if those among the people who had submitted had disbelieved, ﴿لَأسْقَيْناهُمْ﴾ (la-asqaynahum, "We would have given them drink"), as a respite and gradual enticement for them. Using "uprightness" (istiqama) as a metaphor (isti'ara) for disbelief is strained and does not fit. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Jubayr said: it refers to the unjust (al-qasitin), and the meaning is that the path is Islam and truth; ﴿لَأنْعَمْنا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ (la-an'amna 'alayhim, "We would have bestowed favour upon them"), like His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ أنَّ أهْلَ الكِتابِ آمَنُوا واتَّقَوْا﴾ ("And if the People of the Book had believed and feared Allah") [al-Ma'ida: 65], and so on. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَقامُوا﴾ refers to all creation, and ﴿أنْ﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy one.

﴿لَأسْقَيْناهم ماءً غَدَقًا﴾ (la-asqaynahum ma'an ghadaqan, "We would have given them abundant water"): this is a metonymy (kinaya) for the widening of provision, since water is the basis of livelihood. Some said: wealth is where water is. The majority read ﴿غَدَقًا﴾ (ghadaqan) with a fatha on the dal; 'Asim, in the narration of al-A'sha, read it with a kasra. It is said: "the spring flowed abundantly (ghadaqat al-'ayn yughdiqu ghadaqan), so it is ghadiqa," when its water is plentiful. ﴿لِنَفْتِنَهم فِيهِ﴾ (li-naftinahum fihi, "so that We may test them therein"): that is, to test them as to how they will be thankful for what has been bestowed upon them, or to try them and gradually lead them on; and this depends on the disagreement about whom the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَقامُوا﴾ refers to.

Al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read the ﴿و﴾ of ﴿لَوِ﴾ (law) with a damma. The majority read it with a kasra. The Kufans read ﴿يَسْلُكْهُ﴾ (yaslukhu, "He will make him enter") with the ya', and the rest of the seven read it with the nun. Ibn Jundub read it with the nun from aslaka, and some of the Successors (al-tabi'un) read it with the ya' from aslaka as well. Both are dialects: salaka and aslaka. The poet said:

"Until, when they made them enter into Qutaʼida..."

The majority read ﴿صَعَدًا﴾ (sa'adan) with two fathas. It is a verbal noun (dhu masdar) of "sa'ida", used as a description of the punishment; that is, it overpowers the one being punished and dominates him. It was explained as "hardship (shaqq)". It is said: "So-and-so is in sa'ad of his affair", meaning in hardship. 'Umar said: "Nothing weighs on me (yutasa''adu bi) as much as what weighs on me in the marriage sermon," meaning: nothing is burdensome to me. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn 'Abbas said: "ṣaʻad" is a mountain in the Fire. Al-Khudri said: whenever they put their hands upon it, it melts. 'Ikrima said: it is a smooth rock in Hell which one is required to climb; when he reaches its top, he is sent down into Hell. According to this, it may be a substitute (badal) for ﴿عَذابًا﴾ ('adhaban) by omitting a qualifier, meaning "a punishment of ṣaʻad". It may also be that ﴿صَعَدًا﴾ is the object of ﴿يَسْلُكْهُ﴾, and ﴿عَذابًا﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). Some read ﴿صُعُدًا﴾ (su'udan) with two dammas; Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan read it with a damma on the sad and a fatha on the 'ayn. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is that there is no rest in it.

The majority read ﴿وأنَّ المَساجِدَ﴾ (wa-anna al-masajida, "and that the mosques") with a fatha on the hamza, as a coordination (ʻatf) with ﴿أنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ﴾ (annahu istama'a, "that it was he who listened") [al-Jinn: 1], so it is part of what is revealed. Al-Khalil said: the meaning of the verse is "and that the mosques belong to Allah, so do not invoke"; that is, for this reason. Similarly, in his view, ﴿لِإيلافِ قُرَيْشٍ﴾ (li-ilaf Quraysh) [Quraysh: 1] means "so let them worship" (fa-l-ya'budu), and likewise ﴿وأنَّ هَذِهِ أُمَتُّكم﴾ ("and that this your community") means "and because this" (wa-li-anna hadhihi). Ibn Harmaz and Talha read ﴿وإنَّ المَساجِدَ﴾ with a kasra, as a new sentence (isti'naf) and according to al-Khalil's reading; so the meaning is: do not invoke anyone alongside Allah in the mosques, because they belong to Allah alone and are for His worship. The apparent meaning is that the mosques are the houses prepared for prayer and worship in every religious community. Al-Hasan said: every place where prostration is performed is a mosque, whether it was specifically set aside for that or not, because the whole earth is a mosque for this community. Ibn 'Ata' went too far in saying that they are the limbs upon which one prostrates, whose singular is masjad with a fatha on the jim: the forehead, the nose, the two hands, the two knees and the two feet, counting the forehead and nose as one. Also too far is the one who said: "al-Masjid al-Haram", because it is the qibla of mosques, and he said that it is the plural of masjid meaning prostration. It is narrated that it was revealed when Quraysh had overcome the Ka'ba, and it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "All places belong to Allah, so worship Him wherever you are." Ibn Jubayr said: it was revealed because the jinn said: "O Messenger of Allah, how can we attend the prayer with you when we are far from you?" So the verse was revealed to address them with the meaning that your worship is accepted wherever you are, when we enter the mosques.

The majority read ﴿وأنَّهُ لَمّا قامَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ﴾ (wa-annahu lamma qama 'abdu Allah, "and that when the servant of Allah stood") with a fatha on the hamza, as a coordination with their reading ﴿وأنَّ المَساجِدَ﴾ with a fatha. Ibn Harmaz, Talha, Nafi' and Abu Bakr read it with a kasra as a new sentence. ʻAbd Allah is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿يَدْعُوهُ﴾ (yad'uhu, "calling upon Him") means calling upon Allah. ﴿كادُوا﴾ (kadu, "they almost") means the jinn almost. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: they were about to fall upon him to hear the Qur'an. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, in their gathering to reject his message. Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is that this is the saying of the jinn to their people, relating it; and the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾ refers to his companions who followed him and were bound to him in prayer. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why was it not said 'the Messenger of Allah' or 'the Prophet'?" I answer: because its implied meaning is: "And it was revealed to me that when the servant of Allah stood..." and since it occurs within the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about himself, it was phrased in a way that suits humility and self-abasement. Or because the meaning is that the worship of the servant of Allah to Allah is not something far-fetched from reason, nor something so objectionable that they should press upon him in opposition. The meaning of "stood calling upon Him" is "stood worshipping Him," meaning his standing for the dawn prayer at Nakhla when the jinn came to him and listened to his recitation, peace be upon him.

﴿كادُوا يَكُونُونَ عَلَيْهِ لِبَدًا﴾ (kadu yakununa 'alayhi libadan, "they almost became a crowd pressing upon him"): that is, they crowded around him piled upon one another, in wonder at what they saw of his worship and of his companions following him standing, bowing and prostrating, and in admiration of what he recited of the Qur'an, because they saw what they had never seen the like of and heard what they had never heard the like of. End of quotation. This is an earlier view which al-Zamakhshari embellished with his rhetoric. The majority read ﴿لِبَدًا﴾ (libadan) with a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the ba', the plural of libda, like kisra and kisar, meaning groups, likened to a thing matted with parts piled upon one another. From this is the verse of 'Abd Manaf ibn Rib':

"They lined up with six and four hundred tents, until it was as if upon them there was a side (of a crowd) matted together."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "a'wanan" (helpers). Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn 'Amir, in one narration from him, read it with a damma on the lam, the plural of lubda, like zubra and zubur. Also from Ibn Muhaysin: sukun on the ba' and damma on the lam (lubdan). Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Abu Hayya and a group from Abu 'Amr read it with two dammas, as the plural of labd, like rahn and ruhn, or as the plural of labud, like sabur and subur. Al-Hasan and al-Jahdari, in one narration from each, read it (libbadan) with a damma on the lam and a shadda on the ba' with a fatha. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: when the Messenger stood to call, the humans and jinn matted together against this matter to extinguish it, but Allah refused except to give him victory and perfect His light. End of quotation. Those who said that 'Abd Allah here is Nuh (peace be upon him), whose people almost killed him until Allah rescued him from them, were far off the mark; this was said by al-Hasan. Even further off is the view that it is 'Abd Allah ibn Salam.

The majority read: ﴿قالَ إنَّما أدْعُو رَبِّي﴾ (qala innama ad'u rabbi, "He said: I only invoke my Lord"); that is, he said to those who were gathered against him: ﴿إنَّما أدْعُو رَبِّي﴾ ("I only invoke my Lord"), meaning: I have not come to you with a thing to be denied; I only worship my Lord alone, and this is not what should make you unite in enmity against me. Or he said to the jinn, who were crowding in wonder: what you see of the worship of Allah is not a matter to be wondered at; rather, wonder is for one who worships other than Him. Or the jinn said to their people, relating what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said; all of this follows from the disagreement over the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾. ʻAsim, Hamza and Abu 'Amr, in one narration from him, read: ﴿قُلْ﴾ (qul, "Say"); that is, say, O Muhammad, to these who crowd around you, who are either the jinn or the polytheists, according to the two views about the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾.

Then Allah commanded him to say to them what shows his disclaimer of the power to bring them any benefit or harm, and He made harm (darr) the counterpart of right guidance (rushd), expressing by it misguidance (ghayy), since misguidance's result is harm. The meaning may be: harm and no benefit, nor misguidance nor right guidance, so that from each he omitted the counterpart of what indicates it. Al-A'raj read ﴿رُشُدًا﴾ (rushudan) with two dammas. When he (peace be upon him) disclaimed his power to benefit or harm them, he was commanded to inform them that he is a creature (marbub) of Allah Most High, whose Lord does what He wills with him, and that no one can protect him from Him, nor will he find any refuge other than Him to lean upon. Qatada said something close to this. Al-Suddi said: a shelter (hirz). Al-Kalbi said: an entrance into the earth. It was also said: a helper; and it was said: a way and a path, and from this is the poet's saying:

"Alas for my soul! And my soul is of no use to me, and there is no refuge (multahad) from Allah's decree."

It was also said: there is an omission in the speech, which is: they said to him, leave what you call to, and we will protect you; so it was said to him: say, "No one can protect me." It was also said: it is a reply to the words of Wardan, the chief of the jinn, when they were crowded around him: Wardan said, "I will remove them from you," and he said, "No one can protect me," as mentioned by al-Mawardi.

﴿إلّا بَلاغًا﴾ (illa balaghan, "except a conveyance") [al-Jinn: 23]: al-Hasan said: this is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: no one can protect me, but if I convey the message, He will show mercy to me through it. The "protection" (ijara) for conveyance is metaphorical (musta'ara), since it is the cause of Allah's protection and mercy. It was also said that, according to this meaning, it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), meaning: no one can protect me concerning anyone, but I have found nothing to incline to and to hold to except that I convey and obey, so that Allah protects me. So it is permissible to put it in the accusative as an exception from (multahadan), and as a substitute (badal), which is the better view, because what precedes it is a negation; al-Zajjaj construed it as a substitute. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: this exception is disjunctive, because he did not say "and I will not find a refuge," rather he said "besides Him," and conveyance from Allah does not fall under His saying "a refuge besides Him," because it does not come from beside Allah, but from Allah and by His help and His guidance. Qatada said: the implied meaning is: I possess nothing except conveying to you; as for faith and disbelief, I do not possess them. End of quotation. This has a distance to it because of the long separation between the two. It was also said that ﴿إلّا﴾ (illa), in the sense of separation, is: "in" (conditional) and "la" (negative), and its verb is omitted because the verbal noun indicates it; the meaning is: if I do not convey a conveyance from Allah and His message. This is like your saying: "in la qiyaman qu'udan," meaning: if you do not stand in standing, then sit in sitting. The omission of this verb may be because of an indication of it after or before it, as it is omitted in the poet's saying:

"Divorce her, for you are not a match for her, and if not, the sword will reach your forehead."

The estimate: "And if you do not divorce her," where "do not divorce her" (tuṭalliqhā) is omitted because of the indication of "fa-ṭalliqhā" (so divorce her) upon it, and "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya).

Al-Zamakhshari said, following Qatada: meaning, I do not possess [any power] except a conveyance (balāghan) from Allah. And "Say: Indeed, none will protect me from Allah" is a parenthetical sentence (jumla muʿtarida) which he inserted to emphasise the negation of capability from himself and to show his powerlessness, in the sense that: if Allah intends harm to him, such as sickness, death or other than these two, no one can protect him from it, nor find besides Him a refuge to which he may take shelter. End of quote.

(wa-risālātihi) It has been said: it is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "balāghan," meaning: except that I convey from Allah, or I convey His messages. The apparent meaning is that "wa-risālātihi" is a conjunction upon "Allah," meaning: except that I convey from Allah and from His messages.

Ibn Harmaz, Talha, Nafi' and Abu Bakr read it with a kasra as a new sentence. ʻAbd Allah is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿يَدْعُوهُ﴾ (yad'uhu, "calling upon Him") means calling upon Allah. ﴿كادُوا﴾ (kadu, "they almost") means the jinn almost. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: they were about to fall upon him to hear the Qur'an. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, in their gathering to reject his message. Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is that this is the saying of the jinn to their people, relating it; and the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾ refers to his companions who followed him and were bound to him in prayer. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why was it not said 'the Messenger of Allah' or 'the Prophet'?" I answer: because its implied meaning is: "And it was revealed to me that when the servant of Allah stood..." and since it occurs within the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about himself, it was phrased in a way that suits humility and self-abasement. Or because the meaning is that the worship of the servant of Allah to Allah is not something far-fetched from reason, nor something so objectionable that they should press upon him in opposition. The meaning of "stood calling upon Him" is "stood worshipping Him," meaning his standing for the dawn prayer at Nakhla when the jinn came to him and listened to his recitation, peace be upon him.

﴿كادُوا يَكُونُونَ عَلَيْهِ لِبَدًا﴾ (kadu yakununa 'alayhi libadan, "they almost became a crowd pressing upon him"): that is, they crowded around him piled upon one another, in wonder at what they saw of his worship and of his companions following him standing, bowing and prostrating, and in admiration of what he recited of the Qur'an, because they saw what they had never seen the like of and heard what they had never heard the like of. End of quotation. This is an earlier view which al-Zamakhshari embellished with his rhetoric. The majority read ﴿لِبَدًا﴾ (libadan) with a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the ba', the plural of libda, like kisra and kisar, meaning groups, likened to a thing matted with parts piled upon one another. From this is the verse of 'Abd Manaf ibn Rib':

"They lined up with six and four hundred tents, until it was as if upon them there was a side (of a crowd) matted together."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "a'wanan" (helpers). Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn 'Amir, in one narration from him, read it with a damma on the lam, the plural of lubda, like zubra and zubur. Also from Ibn Muhaysin: sukun on the ba' and damma on the lam (lubdan). Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Abu Hayya and a group from Abu 'Amr read it with two dammas, as the plural of labd, like rahn and ruhn, or as the plural of labud, like sabur and subur. Al-Hasan and al-Jahdari, in one narration from each, read it (libbadan) with a damma on the lam and a shadda on the ba' with a fatha. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: when the Messenger stood to call, the humans and jinn matted together against this matter to extinguish it, but Allah refused except to give him victory and perfect His light. End of quotation. Those who said that 'Abd Allah here is Nuh (peace be upon him), whose people almost killed him until Allah rescued him from them, were far off the mark; this was said by al-Hasan. Even further off is the view that it is 'Abd Allah ibn Salam.

The majority read: ﴿قالَ إنَّما أدْعُو رَبِّي﴾ (qala innama ad'u rabbi, "He said: I only invoke my Lord"); that is, he said to those who were gathered against him: ﴿إنَّما أدْعُو رَبِّي﴾ ("I only invoke my Lord"), meaning: I have not come to you with a thing to be denied; I only worship my Lord alone, and this is not what should make you unite in enmity against me. Or he said to the jinn, who were crowding in wonder: what you see of the worship of Allah is not a matter to be wondered at; rather, wonder is for one who worships other than Him. Or the jinn said to their people, relating what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said; all of this follows from the disagreement over the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾. ʻAsim, Hamza and Abu 'Amr, in one narration from him, read: ﴿قُلْ﴾ (qul, "Say"); that is, say, O Muhammad, to these who crowd around you, who are either the jinn or the polytheists, according to the two views about the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾.

Then Allah commanded him to say to them what shows his disclaimer of the power to bring them any benefit or harm, and He made harm (darr) the counterpart of right guidance (rushd), expressing by it misguidance (ghayy), since misguidance's result is harm. The meaning may be: harm and no benefit, nor misguidance nor right guidance, so that from each he omitted the counterpart of what indicates it. Al-A'raj read ﴿رُشُدًا﴾ (rushudan) with two dammas. When he (peace be upon him) disclaimed his power to benefit or harm them, he was commanded to inform them that he is a creature (marbub) of Allah Most High, whose Lord does what He wills with him, and that no one can protect him from Him, nor will he find any refuge other than Him to lean upon. Qatada said something close to this. Al-Suddi said: a shelter (hirz). Al-Kalbi said: an entrance into the earth. It was also said: a helper; and it was said: a way and a path, and from this is the poet's saying:

"Alas for my soul! And my soul is of no use to me, and there is no refuge (multahad) from Allah's decree."

It was also said: there is an omission in the speech, which is: they said to him, leave what you call to, and we will protect you; so it was said to him: say, "No one can protect me." It was also said: it is a reply to the words of Wardan, the chief of the jinn, when they were crowded around him: Wardan said, "I will remove them from you," and he said, "No one can protect me," as mentioned by al-Mawardi.

﴿إلّا بَلاغًا﴾ (illa balaghan, "except a conveyance") [al-Jinn: 23]: al-Hasan said: this is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: no one can protect me, but if I convey the message, He will show mercy to me through it. The "protection" (ijara) for conveyance is metaphorical (musta'ara), since it is the cause of Allah's protection and mercy. It was also said that, according to this meaning, it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), meaning: no one can protect me concerning anyone, but I have found nothing to incline to and to hold to except that I convey and obey, so that Allah protects me. So it is permissible to put it in the accusative as an exception from (multahadan), and as a substitute (badal), which is the better view, because what precedes it is a negation; al-Zajjaj construed it as a substitute. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: this exception is disjunctive, because he did not say "and I will not find a refuge," rather he said "besides Him," and conveyance from Allah does not fall under His saying "a refuge besides Him," because it does not come from beside Allah, but from Allah and by His help and His guidance. Qatada said: the implied meaning is: I possess nothing except conveying to you; as for faith and disbelief, I do not possess them. End of quotation. This has a distance to it because of the long separation between the two. It was also said that ﴿إلّا﴾ (illa), in the sense of separation, is: "in" (conditional) and "la" (negative), and its verb is omitted because the verbal noun indicates it; the meaning is: if I do not convey a conveyance from Allah and His message. This is like your saying: "in la qiyaman qu'udan," meaning: if you do not stand in standing, then sit in sitting. The omission of this verb may be because of an indication of it after or before it, as it is omitted in the poet's saying:

"Divorce her, for you are not a match for her, and if not, the sword will reach your forehead."

The estimate: "And if you do not divorce her," where "do not divorce her" (tuṭalliqhā) is omitted because of the indication of "fa-ṭalliqhā" (so divorce her) upon it, and "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya).

Al-Zamakhshari said, following Qatada: meaning, I do not possess [any power] except a conveyance (balāghan) from Allah. And "Say: Indeed, none will protect me from Allah" is a parenthetical sentence (jumla muʿtarida) which he inserted to emphasise the negation of capability from himself and to show his powerlessness, in the sense that: if Allah intends harm to him, such as sickness, death or other than these two, no one can protect him from it, nor find besides Him a refuge to which he may take shelter. End of quote.

(wa-risālātihi) It has been said: it is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "balāghan," meaning: except that I convey from Allah, or I convey His messages. The apparent meaning is that "wa-risālātihi" is a conjunction upon "Allah," meaning: except that I convey from Allah and from His messages.

﴿And that if they had remained upright on the path, We would have given them abundant water﴾ [al-Jinn: 16]. ﴿So that We might test them therein. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a severe punishment﴾ [al-Jinn: 17]. ﴿And that the mosques belong to Allah, so do not invoke anyone alongside Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18]. ﴿And that when the servant of Allah stood calling upon Him, they almost became a crowd pressing upon him﴾ [al-Jinn: 19]. ﴿Say: "I only invoke my Lord and associate no one with Him"﴾ [al-Jinn: 20]. ﴿Say: "I do not possess for you any harm or any right guidance"﴾ [al-Jinn: 21]. ﴿Say: "No one can protect me from Allah, nor will I find any refuge besides Him"﴾ [al-Jinn: 22], ﴿except a conveyance from Allah and His messages. And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, indeed, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn: 23]. ﴿Until, when they see what they are promised, they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number﴾ [al-Jinn: 24]. ﴿Say: "I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will set for it a long term"﴾ [al-Jinn: 25]. ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone﴾ [al-Jinn: 26], ﴿except one whom He has approved of among messengers; indeed, He sends before him and behind him guards﴾ [al-Jinn: 27], ﴿so that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord. And He has encompassed what is with them and has enumerated everything in number﴾ [al-Jinn: 28].

This is part of what is revealed under ﴿It has been revealed to me﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]. The word ﴿أنْ﴾ (an) is the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy ﴿inna﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَقامُوا﴾ (istaqamu, "they remained upright") refers to the following. Al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Zayd ibn Aslam and Abu Mijlaz said: it refers to the words ﴿فَمَن أسْلَمَ﴾ (fa-man aslama, "whoever submits") [al-Jinn: 14], and "the path" (al-tariqa) is the path of disbelief; that is, if those among the people who had submitted had disbelieved, ﴿لَأسْقَيْناهُمْ﴾ (la-asqaynahum, "We would have given them drink"), as a respite and gradual enticement for them. Using "uprightness" (istiqama) as a metaphor (isti'ara) for disbelief is strained and does not fit. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Jubayr said: it refers to the unjust (al-qasitin), and the meaning is that the path is Islam and truth; ﴿لَأنْعَمْنا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ (la-an'amna 'alayhim, "We would have bestowed favour upon them"), like His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ أنَّ أهْلَ الكِتابِ آمَنُوا واتَّقَوْا﴾ ("And if the People of the Book had believed and feared Allah") [al-Ma'ida: 65], and so on. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَقامُوا﴾ refers to all creation, and ﴿أنْ﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy one.

﴿لَأسْقَيْناهم ماءً غَدَقًا﴾ (la-asqaynahum ma'an ghadaqan, "We would have given them abundant water"): this is a metonymy (kinaya) for the widening of provision, since water is the basis of livelihood. Some said: wealth is where water is. The majority read ﴿غَدَقًا﴾ (ghadaqan) with a fatha on the dal; 'Asim, in the narration of al-A'sha, read it with a kasra. It is said: "the spring flowed abundantly (ghadaqat al-'ayn yughdiqu ghadaqan), so it is ghadiqa," when its water is plentiful. ﴿لِنَفْتِنَهم فِيهِ﴾ (li-naftinahum fihi, "so that We may test them therein"): that is, to test them as to how they will be thankful for what has been bestowed upon them, or to try them and gradually lead them on; and this depends on the disagreement about whom the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَقامُوا﴾ refers to.

Al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read the ﴿و﴾ of ﴿لَوِ﴾ (law) with a damma. The majority read it with a kasra. The Kufans read ﴿يَسْلُكْهُ﴾ (yaslukhu, "He will make him enter") with the ya', and the rest of the seven read it with the nun. Ibn Jundub read it with the nun from aslaka, and some of the Successors (al-tabi'un) read it with the ya' from aslaka as well. Both are dialects: salaka and aslaka. The poet said:

"Until, when they made them enter into Qutaʼida..."

The majority read ﴿صَعَدًا﴾ (sa'adan) with two fathas. It is a verbal noun (dhu masdar) of "sa'ida", used as a description of the punishment; that is, it overpowers the one being punished and dominates him. It was explained as "hardship (shaqq)". It is said: "So-and-so is in sa'ad of his affair", meaning in hardship. 'Umar said: "Nothing weighs on me (yutasa''adu bi) as much as what weighs on me in the marriage sermon," meaning: nothing is burdensome to me. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn 'Abbas said: "ṣaʻad" is a mountain in the Fire. Al-Khudri said: whenever they put their hands upon it, it melts. 'Ikrima said: it is a smooth rock in Hell which one is required to climb; when he reaches its top, he is sent down into Hell. According to this, it may be a substitute (badal) for ﴿عَذابًا﴾ ('adhaban) by omitting a qualifier, meaning "a punishment of ṣaʻad". It may also be that ﴿صَعَدًا﴾ is the object of ﴿يَسْلُكْهُ﴾, and ﴿عَذابًا﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). Some read ﴿صُعُدًا﴾ (su'udan) with two dammas; Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan read it with a damma on the sad and a fatha on the 'ayn. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is that there is no rest in it.

The majority read ﴿وأنَّ المَساجِدَ﴾ (wa-anna al-masajida, "and that the mosques") with a fatha on the hamza, as a coordination (ʻatf) with ﴿أنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ﴾ (annahu istama'a, "that it was he who listened") [al-Jinn: 1], so it is part of what is revealed. Al-Khalil said: the meaning of the verse is "and that the mosques belong to Allah, so do not invoke"; that is, for this reason. Similarly, in his view, ﴿لِإيلافِ قُرَيْشٍ﴾ (li-ilaf Quraysh) [Quraysh: 1] means "so let them worship" (fa-l-ya'budu), and likewise ﴿وأنَّ هَذِهِ أُمَتُّكم﴾ ("and that this your community") means "and because this" (wa-li-anna hadhihi). Ibn Harmaz and Talha read ﴿وإنَّ المَساجِدَ﴾ with a kasra, as a new sentence (isti'naf) and according to al-Khalil's reading; so the meaning is: do not invoke anyone alongside Allah in the mosques, because they belong to Allah alone and are for His worship. The apparent meaning is that the mosques are the houses prepared for prayer and worship in every religious community. Al-Hasan said: every place where prostration is performed is a mosque, whether it was specifically set aside for that or not, because the whole earth is a mosque for this community. Ibn 'Ata' went too far in saying that they are the limbs upon which one prostrates, whose singular is masjad with a fatha on the jim: the forehead, the nose, the two hands, the two knees and the two feet, counting the forehead and nose as one. Also too far is the one who said: "al-Masjid al-Haram", because it is the qibla of mosques, and he said that it is the plural of masjid meaning prostration. It is narrated that it was revealed when Quraysh had overcome the Ka'ba, and it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "All places belong to Allah, so worship Him wherever you are." Ibn Jubayr said: it was revealed because the jinn said: "O Messenger of Allah, how can we attend the prayer with you when we are far from you?" So the verse was revealed to address them with the meaning that your worship is accepted wherever you are, when we enter the mosques.

﴿And that if they had remained upright on the path, We would have given them abundant water﴾ [al-Jinn: 16]. ﴿So that We might test them therein. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a severe punishment﴾ [al-Jinn: 17]. ﴿And that the mosques belong to Allah, so do not invoke anyone alongside Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18]. ﴿And that when the servant of Allah stood calling upon Him, they almost became a crowd pressing upon him﴾ [al-Jinn: 19]. ﴿Say: "I only invoke my Lord and associate no one with Him"﴾ [al-Jinn: 20]. ﴿Say: "I do not possess for you any harm or any right guidance"﴾ [al-Jinn: 21]. ﴿Say: "No one can protect me from Allah, nor will I find any refuge besides Him"﴾ [al-Jinn: 22], ﴿except a conveyance from Allah and His messages. And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, indeed, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn: 23]. ﴿Until, when they see what they are promised, they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number﴾ [al-Jinn: 24]. ﴿Say: "I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will set for it a long term"﴾ [al-Jinn: 25]. ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone﴾ [al-Jinn: 26], ﴿except one whom He has approved of among messengers; indeed, He sends before him and behind him guards﴾ [al-Jinn: 27], ﴿so that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord. And He has encompassed what is with them and has enumerated everything in number﴾ [al-Jinn: 28].

This is part of what is revealed under ﴿It has been revealed to me﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]. The word ﴿أنْ﴾ (an) is the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy ﴿inna﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَقامُوا﴾ (istaqamu, "they remained upright") refers to the following. Al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Zayd ibn Aslam and Abu Mijlaz said: it refers to the words ﴿فَمَن أسْلَمَ﴾ (fa-man aslama, "whoever submits") [al-Jinn: 14], and "the path" (al-tariqa) is the path of disbelief; that is, if those among the people who had submitted had disbelieved, ﴿لَأسْقَيْناهُمْ﴾ (la-asqaynahum, "We would have given them drink"), as a respite and gradual enticement for them. According to this, it may be a substitute (badal) for ﴿عَذابًا﴾ ('adhaban) by omitting a qualifier, meaning "a punishment of ṣaʻad". Al-Hasan said: every place where prostration is performed is a mosque, whether it was specifically set aside for that or not, because the whole earth is a mosque for this community. Ibn 'Ata' went too far in saying that they are the limbs upon which one prostrates, whose singular is masjad with a fatha on the jim: the forehead, the nose, the two hands, the two knees and the two feet, counting the forehead and nose as one. Also too far is the one who said: "al-Masjid al-Haram", because it is the qibla of mosques, and he said that it is the plural of masjid meaning prostration. It is narrated that it was revealed when Quraysh had overcome the Ka'ba, and it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "All places belong to Allah, so worship Him wherever you are." Ibn Jubayr said: it was revealed because the jinn said: "O Messenger of Allah, how can we attend the prayer with you when we are far from you?" So the verse was revealed to address them with the meaning that your worship is accepted wherever you are, when we enter the mosques.

The majority read ﴿وأنَّهُ لَمّا قامَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ﴾ (wa-annahu lamma qama 'abdu Allah, "and that when the servant of Allah stood") with a fatha on the hamza, as a coordination with their reading ﴿وأنَّ المَساجِدَ﴾ with a fatha. Ibn Harmaz, Talha, Nafi' and Abu Bakr read it with a kasra as a new sentence. ʻAbd Allah is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿يَدْعُوهُ﴾ (yad'uhu, "calling upon Him") means calling upon Allah. ﴿كادُوا﴾ (kadu, "they almost") means the jinn almost. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: they were about to fall upon him to hear the Qur'an. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, in their gathering to reject his message. Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is that this is the saying of the jinn to their people, relating it; and the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾ refers to his companions who followed him and were bound to him in prayer. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why was it not said 'the Messenger of Allah' or 'the Prophet'?" I answer: because its implied meaning is: "And it was revealed to me that when the servant of Allah stood..." and since it occurs within the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about himself, it was phrased in a way that suits humility and self-abasement. Or because the meaning is that the worship of the servant of Allah to Allah is not something far-fetched from reason, nor something so objectionable that they should press upon him in opposition. The meaning of "stood calling upon Him" is "stood worshipping Him," meaning his standing for the dawn prayer at Nakhla when the jinn came to him and listened to his recitation, peace be upon him.

﴿كادُوا يَكُونُونَ عَلَيْهِ لِبَدًا﴾ (kadu yakununa 'alayhi libadan, "they almost became a crowd pressing upon him"): that is, they crowded around him piled upon one another, in wonder at what they saw of his worship and of his companions following him standing, bowing and prostrating, and in admiration of what he recited of the Qur'an, because they saw what they had never seen the like of and heard what they had never heard the like of. End of quotation. This is an earlier view which al-Zamakhshari embellished with his rhetoric. The majority read ﴿لِبَدًا﴾ (libadan) with a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the ba', the plural of libda, like kisra and kisar, meaning groups, likened to a thing matted with parts piled upon one another. From this is the verse of 'Abd Manaf ibn Rib':

"They lined up with six and four hundred tents, until it was as if upon them there was a side (of a crowd) matted together."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "a'wanan" (helpers). Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn 'Amir, in one narration from him, read it with a damma on the lam, the plural of lubda, like zubra and zubur. Also from Ibn Muhaysin: sukun on the ba' and damma on the lam (lubdan). Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Abu Hayya and a group from Abu 'Amr read it with two dammas, as the plural of labd, like rahn and ruhn, or as the plural of labud, like sabur and subur. Al-Hasan and al-Jahdari, in one narration from each, read it (libbadan) with a damma on the lam and a shadda on the ba' with a fatha. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: when the Messenger stood to call, the humans and jinn matted together against this matter to extinguish it, but Allah refused except to give him victory and perfect His light. End of quotation. Those who said that 'Abd Allah here is Nuh (peace be upon him), whose people almost killed him until Allah rescued him from them, were far off the mark; this was said by al-Hasan. Even further off is the view that it is 'Abd Allah ibn Salam.

The majority read: ﴿قالَ إنَّما أدْعُو رَبِّي﴾ (qala innama ad'u rabbi, "He said: I only invoke my Lord"); that is, he said to those who were gathered against him: ﴿إنَّما أدْعُو رَبِّي﴾ ("I only invoke my Lord"), meaning: I have not come to you with a thing to be denied; I only worship my Lord alone, and this is not what should make you unite in enmity against me. Or he said to the jinn, who were crowding in wonder: what you see of the worship of Allah is not a matter to be wondered at; rather, wonder is for one who worships other than Him. Or the jinn said to their people, relating what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said; all of this follows from the disagreement over the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾. ʻAsim, Hamza and Abu 'Amr, in one narration from him, read: ﴿قُلْ﴾ (qul, "Say"); that is, say, O Muhammad, to these who crowd around you, who are either the jinn or the polytheists, according to the two views about the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾.

Then Allah commanded him to say to them what shows his disclaimer of the power to bring them any benefit or harm, and He made harm (darr) the counterpart of right guidance (rushd), expressing by it misguidance (ghayy), since misguidance's result is harm. The meaning may be: harm and no benefit, nor misguidance nor right guidance, so that from each he omitted the counterpart of what indicates it. Al-A'raj read ﴿رُشُدًا﴾ (rushudan) with two dammas. When he (peace be upon him) disclaimed his power to benefit or harm them, he was commanded to inform them that he is a creature (marbub) of Allah Most High, whose Lord does what He wills with him, and that no one can protect him from Him, nor will he find any refuge other than Him to lean upon. Qatada said something close to this. Al-Suddi said: a shelter (hirz). Al-Kalbi said: an entrance into the earth. It was also said: a helper; and it was said: a way and a path, and from this is the poet's saying:

"Alas for my soul! And my soul is of no use to me, and there is no refuge (multahad) from Allah's decree."

It was also said: there is an omission in the speech, which is: they said to him, leave what you call to, and we will protect you; so it was said to him: say, "No one can protect me." It was also said: it is a reply to the words of Wardan, the chief of the jinn, when they were crowded around him: Wardan said, "I will remove them from you," and he said, "No one can protect me," as mentioned by al-Mawardi.

﴿إلّا بَلاغًا﴾ (illa balaghan, "except a conveyance") [al-Jinn: 23]: al-Hasan said: this is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: no one can protect me, but if I convey the message, He will show mercy to me through it. The "protection" (ijara) for conveyance is metaphorical (musta'ara), since it is the cause of Allah's protection and mercy. It was also said that, according to this meaning, it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), meaning: no one can protect me concerning anyone, but I have found nothing to incline to and to hold to except that I convey and obey, so that Allah protects me. So it is permissible to put it in the accusative as an exception from (multahadan), and as a substitute (badal), which is the better view, because what precedes it is a negation; al-Zajjaj construed it as a substitute. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: this exception is disjunctive, because he did not say "and I will not find a refuge," rather he said "besides Him," and conveyance from Allah does not fall under His saying "a refuge besides Him," because it does not come from beside Allah, but from Allah and by His help and His guidance. Qatada said: the implied meaning is: I possess nothing except conveying to you; as for faith and disbelief, I do not possess them. End of quotation. This has a distance to it because of the long separation between the two. It was also said that ﴿إلّا﴾ (illa), in the sense of separation, is: "in" (conditional) and "la" (negative), and its verb is omitted because the verbal noun indicates it; the meaning is: if I do not convey a conveyance from Allah and His message. This is like your saying: "in la qiyaman qu'udan," meaning: if you do not stand in standing, then sit in sitting. The omission of this verb may be because of an indication of it after or before it, as it is omitted in the poet's saying:

"Divorce her, for you are not a match for her, and if not, the sword will reach your forehead."

The estimate: "And if you do not divorce her," where "do not divorce her" (tuṭalliqhā) is omitted because of the indication of "fa-ṭalliqhā" (so divorce her) upon it, and "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya).

Al-Zamakhshari said, following Qatada: meaning, I do not possess [any power] except a conveyance (balāghan) from Allah. And "Say: Indeed, none will protect me from Allah" is a parenthetical sentence (jumla muʿtarida) which he inserted to emphasise the negation of capability from himself and to show his powerlessness, in the sense that: if Allah intends harm to him, such as sickness, death or other than these two, no one can protect him from it, nor find besides Him a refuge to which he may take shelter. End of quote.

The majority read ﴿وأنَّهُ لَمّا قامَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ﴾ (wa-annahu lamma qama 'abdu Allah, "and that when the servant of Allah stood") with a fatha on the hamza, as a coordination with their reading ﴿وأنَّ المَساجِدَ﴾ with a fatha. Ibn Harmaz, Talha, Nafi' and Abu Bakr read it with a kasra as a new sentence. ʻAbd Allah is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿يَدْعُوهُ﴾ (yad'uhu, "calling upon Him") means calling upon Allah. ﴿كادُوا﴾ (kadu, "they almost") means the jinn almost. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: they were about to fall upon him to hear the Qur'an. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, in their gathering to reject his message. Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is that this is the saying of the jinn to their people, relating it; and the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾ refers to his companions who followed him and were bound to him in prayer. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why was it not said 'the Messenger of Allah' or 'the Prophet'?" I answer: because its implied meaning is: "And it was revealed to me that when the servant of Allah stood..." and since it occurs within the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about himself, it was phrased in a way that suits humility and self-abasement. Or because the meaning is that the worship of the servant of Allah to Allah is not something far-fetched from reason, nor something so objectionable that they should press upon him in opposition. The meaning of "stood calling upon Him" is "stood worshipping Him," meaning his standing for the dawn prayer at Nakhla when the jinn came to him and listened to his recitation, peace be upon him.

﴿كادُوا يَكُونُونَ عَلَيْهِ لِبَدًا﴾ (kadu yakununa 'alayhi libadan, "they almost became a crowd pressing upon him"): that is, they crowded around him piled upon one another, in wonder at what they saw of his worship and of his companions following him standing, bowing and prostrating, and in admiration of what he recited of the Qur'an, because they saw what they had never seen the like of and heard what they had never heard the like of. End of quotation. This is an earlier view which al-Zamakhshari embellished with his rhetoric. The majority read ﴿لِبَدًا﴾ (libadan) with a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the ba', the plural of libda, like kisra and kisar, meaning groups, likened to a thing matted with parts piled upon one another. From this is the verse of 'Abd Manaf ibn Rib':

"They lined up with six and four hundred tents, until it was as if upon them there was a side (of a crowd) matted together."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "a'wanan" (helpers). Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn 'Amir, in one narration from him, read it with a damma on the lam, the plural of lubda, like zubra and zubur. Also from Ibn Muhaysin: sukun on the ba' and damma on the lam (lubdan). Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Abu Hayya and a group from Abu 'Amr read it with two dammas, as the plural of labd, like rahn and ruhn, or as the plural of labud, like sabur and subur. Al-Hasan and al-Jahdari, in one narration from each, read it (libbadan) with a damma on the lam and a shadda on the ba' with a fatha. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: when the Messenger stood to call, the humans and jinn matted together against this matter to extinguish it, but Allah refused except to give him victory and perfect His light. End of quotation. Those who said that 'Abd Allah here is Nuh (peace be upon him), whose people almost killed him until Allah rescued him from them, were far off the mark; this was said by al-Hasan. Even further off is the view that it is 'Abd Allah ibn Salam.

The majority read: ﴿قالَ إنَّما أدْعُو رَبِّي﴾ (qala innama ad'u rabbi, "He said: I only invoke my Lord"); that is, he said to those who were gathered against him: ﴿إنَّما أدْعُو رَبِّي﴾ ("I only invoke my Lord"), meaning: I have not come to you with a thing to be denied; I only worship my Lord alone, and this is not what should make you unite in enmity against me. Or he said to the jinn, who were crowding in wonder: what you see of the worship of Allah is not a matter to be wondered at; rather, wonder is for one who worships other than Him. Or the jinn said to their people, relating what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said; all of this follows from the disagreement over the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾. ʻAsim, Hamza and Abu 'Amr, in one narration from him, read: ﴿قُلْ﴾ (qul, "Say"); that is, say, O Muhammad, to these who crowd around you, who are either the jinn or the polytheists, according to the two views about the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾.

Then Allah commanded him to say to them what shows his disclaimer of the power to bring them any benefit or harm, and He made harm (darr) the counterpart of right guidance (rushd), expressing by it misguidance (ghayy), since misguidance's result is harm. The meaning may be: harm and no benefit, nor misguidance nor right guidance, so that from each he omitted the counterpart of what indicates it. Al-A'raj read ﴿رُشُدًا﴾ (rushudan) with two dammas. When he (peace be upon him) disclaimed his power to benefit or harm them, he was commanded to inform them that he is a creature (marbub) of Allah Most High, whose Lord does what He wills with him, and that no one can protect him from Him, nor will he find any refuge other than Him to lean upon. Qatada said something close to this. Al-Suddi said: a shelter (hirz). Al-Kalbi said: an entrance into the earth. It was also said: a helper; and it was said: a way and a path, and from this is the poet's saying:

"Alas for my soul! And my soul is of no use to me, and there is no refuge (multahad) from Allah's decree."

It was also said: there is an omission in the speech, which is: they said to him, leave what you call to, and we will protect you; so it was said to him: say, "No one can protect me." It was also said: it is a reply to the words of Wardan, the chief of the jinn, when they were crowded around him: Wardan said, "I will remove them from you," and he said, "No one can protect me," as mentioned by al-Mawardi.

﴿إلّا بَلاغًا﴾ (illa balaghan, "except a conveyance") [al-Jinn: 23]: al-Hasan said: this is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: no one can protect me, but if I convey the message, He will show mercy to me through it. The "protection" (ijara) for conveyance is metaphorical (musta'ara), since it is the cause of Allah's protection and mercy. It was also said that, according to this meaning, it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), meaning: no one can protect me concerning anyone, but I have found nothing to incline to and to hold to except that I convey and obey, so that Allah protects me. So it is permissible to put it in the accusative as an exception from (multahadan), and as a substitute (badal), which is the better view, because what precedes it is a negation; al-Zajjaj construed it as a substitute. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: this exception is disjunctive, because he did not say "and I will not find a refuge," rather he said "besides Him," and conveyance from Allah does not fall under His saying "a refuge besides Him," because it does not come from beside Allah, but from Allah and by His help and His guidance. Qatada said: the implied meaning is: I possess nothing except conveying to you; as for faith and disbelief, I do not possess them. End of quotation. This has a distance to it because of the long separation between the two. It was also said that ﴿إلّا﴾ (illa), in the sense of separation, is: "in" (conditional) and "la" (negative), and its verb is omitted because the verbal noun indicates it; the meaning is: if I do not convey a conveyance from Allah and His message. This is like your saying: "in la qiyaman qu'udan," meaning: if you do not stand in standing, then sit in sitting. The omission of this verb may be because of an indication of it after or before it, as it is omitted in the poet's saying:

"Divorce her, for you are not a match for her, and if not, the sword will reach your forehead."

The estimate: "And if you do not divorce her," where "do not divorce her" (tuṭalliqhā) is omitted because of the indication of "fa-ṭalliqhā" (so divorce her) upon it, and "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya).

Al-Zamakhshari said, following Qatada: meaning, I do not possess [any power] except a conveyance (balāghan) from Allah. And "Say: Indeed, none will protect me from Allah" is a parenthetical sentence (jumla muʿtarida) which he inserted to emphasise the negation of capability from himself and to show his powerlessness, in the sense that: if Allah intends harm to him, such as sickness, death or other than these two, no one can protect him from it, nor find besides Him a refuge to which he may take shelter. End of quote.

(wa-risālātihi) It has been said: it is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "balāghan," meaning: except that I convey from Allah, or I convey His messages. The apparent meaning is that "wa-risālātihi" is a conjunction upon "Allah," meaning: except that I convey from Allah and from His messages.

﴿And that if they had remained upright on the path, We would have given them abundant water﴾ [al-Jinn: 16]. ﴿So that We might test them therein. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a severe punishment﴾ [al-Jinn: 17]. ﴿And that the mosques belong to Allah, so do not invoke anyone alongside Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18]. ﴿And that when the servant of Allah stood calling upon Him, they almost became a crowd pressing upon him﴾ [al-Jinn: 19]. ﴿Say: "I only invoke my Lord and associate no one with Him"﴾ [al-Jinn: 20]. ﴿Say: "I do not possess for you any harm or any right guidance"﴾ [al-Jinn: 21]. ﴿Say: "No one can protect me from Allah, nor will I find any refuge besides Him"﴾ [al-Jinn: 22], ﴿except a conveyance from Allah and His messages. And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, indeed, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn: 23]. ﴿Until, when they see what they are promised, they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number﴾ [al-Jinn: 24]. ﴿Say: "I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will set for it a long term"﴾ [al-Jinn: 25]. ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone﴾ [al-Jinn: 26], ﴿except one whom He has approved of among messengers; indeed, He sends before him and behind him guards﴾ [al-Jinn: 27], ﴿so that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord. And He has encompassed what is with them and has enumerated everything in number﴾ [al-Jinn: 28].

This is part of what is revealed under ﴿It has been revealed to me﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]. The word ﴿أنْ﴾ (an) is the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy ﴿inna﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَقامُوا﴾ (istaqamu, "they remained upright") refers to the following. Al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Zayd ibn Aslam and Abu Mijlaz said: it refers to the words ﴿فَمَن أسْلَمَ﴾ (fa-man aslama, "whoever submits") [al-Jinn: 14], and "the path" (al-tariqa) is the path of disbelief; that is, if those among the people who had submitted had disbelieved, ﴿لَأسْقَيْناهُمْ﴾ (la-asqaynahum, "We would have given them drink"), as a respite and gradual enticement for them. Using "uprightness" (istiqama) as a metaphor (isti'ara) for disbelief is strained and does not fit. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Jubayr said: it refers to the unjust (al-qasitin), and the meaning is that the path is Islam and truth; ﴿لَأنْعَمْنا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ (la-an'amna 'alayhim, "We would have bestowed favour upon them"), like His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ أنَّ أهْلَ الكِتابِ آمَنُوا واتَّقَوْا﴾ ("And if the People of the Book had believed and feared Allah") [al-Ma'ida: 65], and so on. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَقامُوا﴾ refers to all creation, and ﴿أنْ﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy one.

﴿لَأسْقَيْناهم ماءً غَدَقًا﴾ (la-asqaynahum ma'an ghadaqan, "We would have given them abundant water"): this is a metonymy (kinaya) for the widening of provision, since water is the basis of livelihood. Some said: wealth is where water is. The majority read ﴿غَدَقًا﴾ (ghadaqan) with a fatha on the dal; 'Asim, in the narration of al-A'sha, read it with a kasra. It is said: "the spring flowed abundantly (ghadaqat al-'ayn yughdiqu ghadaqan), so it is ghadiqa," when its water is plentiful. ﴿لِنَفْتِنَهم فِيهِ﴾ (li-naftinahum fihi, "so that We may test them therein"): that is, to test them as to how they will be thankful for what has been bestowed upon them, or to try them and gradually lead them on; and this depends on the disagreement about whom the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَقامُوا﴾ refers to.

Al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read the ﴿و﴾ of ﴿لَوِ﴾ (law) with a damma. The majority read it with a kasra. The Kufans read ﴿يَسْلُكْهُ﴾ (yaslukhu, "He will make him enter") with the ya', and the rest of the seven read it with the nun. Ibn Jundub read it with the nun from aslaka, and some of the Successors (al-tabi'un) read it with the ya' from aslaka as well. Both are dialects: salaka and aslaka. The poet said:

"Until, when they made them enter into Qutaʼida..."

The majority read ﴿صَعَدًا﴾ (sa'adan) with two fathas. It is a verbal noun (dhu masdar) of "sa'ida", used as a description of the punishment; that is, it overpowers the one being punished and dominates him. It was explained as "hardship (shaqq)". It is said: "So-and-so is in sa'ad of his affair", meaning in hardship. 'Umar said: "Nothing weighs on me (yutasa''adu bi) as much as what weighs on me in the marriage sermon," meaning: nothing is burdensome to me. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn 'Abbas said: "ṣaʻad" is a mountain in the Fire. Al-Khudri said: whenever they put their hands upon it, it melts. 'Ikrima said: it is a smooth rock in Hell which one is required to climb; when he reaches its top, he is sent down into Hell. According to this, it may be a substitute (badal) for ﴿عَذابًا﴾ ('adhaban) by omitting a qualifier, meaning "a punishment of ṣaʻad". It may also be that ﴿صَعَدًا﴾ is the object of ﴿يَسْلُكْهُ﴾, and ﴿عَذابًا﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). Some read ﴿صُعُدًا﴾ (su'udan) with two dammas; Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan read it with a damma on the sad and a fatha on the 'ayn. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is that there is no rest in it.

The majority read ﴿وأنَّ المَساجِدَ﴾ (wa-anna al-masajida, "and that the mosques") with a fatha on the hamza, as a coordination (ʻatf) with ﴿أنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ﴾ (annahu istama'a, "that it was he who listened") [al-Jinn: 1], so it is part of what is revealed. Al-Khalil said: the meaning of the verse is "and that the mosques belong to Allah, so do not invoke"; that is, for this reason. Similarly, in his view, ﴿لِإيلافِ قُرَيْشٍ﴾ (li-ilaf Quraysh) [Quraysh: 1] means "so let them worship" (fa-l-ya'budu), and likewise ﴿وأنَّ هَذِهِ أُمَتُّكم﴾ ("and that this your community") means "and because this" (wa-li-anna hadhihi). Ibn Harmaz and Talha read ﴿وإنَّ المَساجِدَ﴾ with a kasra, as a new sentence (isti'naf) and according to al-Khalil's reading; so the meaning is: do not invoke anyone alongside Allah in the mosques, because they belong to Allah alone and are for His worship. The apparent meaning is that the mosques are the houses prepared for prayer and worship in every religious community. Al-Hasan said: every place where prostration is performed is a mosque, whether it was specifically set aside for that or not, because the whole earth is a mosque for this community. Ibn 'Ata' went too far in saying that they are the limbs upon which one prostrates, whose singular is masjad with a fatha on the jim: the forehead, the nose, the two hands, the two knees and the two feet, counting the forehead and nose as one. Also too far is the one who said: "al-Masjid al-Haram", because it is the qibla of mosques, and he said that it is the plural of masjid meaning prostration. It is narrated that it was revealed when Quraysh had overcome the Ka'ba, and it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "All places belong to Allah, so worship Him wherever you are." Ibn Jubayr said: it was revealed because the jinn said: "O Messenger of Allah, how can we attend the prayer with you when we are far from you?" So the verse was revealed to address them with the meaning that your worship is accepted wherever you are, when we enter the mosques.
