And "Say: Indeed, none will protect me from Allah" is a parenthetical sentence (jumla muʿtarida) which he inserted to emphasise the negation of capability from himself and to show his powerlessness, in the sense that: if Allah intends harm to him, such as sickness, death or other than these two, no one can protect him from it, nor find besides Him a refuge to which he may take shelter. End of quote.

(wa-risālātihi) It has been said: it is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "balāghan," meaning: except that I convey from Allah, or I convey His messages. The apparent meaning is that "wa-risālātihi" is a conjunction upon "Allah," meaning: except that I convey from Allah and from His messages.

﴿And that if they had remained upright on the path, We would have given them abundant water﴾ [al-Jinn: 16]. ﴿So that We might test them therein. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a severe punishment﴾ [al-Jinn: 17]. ﴿And that the mosques belong to Allah, so do not invoke anyone alongside Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18]. ﴿And that when the servant of Allah stood calling upon Him, they almost became a crowd pressing upon him﴾ [al-Jinn: 19]. ﴿Say: "I only invoke my Lord and associate no one with Him"﴾ [al-Jinn: 20]. ﴿Say: "I do not possess for you any harm or any right guidance"﴾ [al-Jinn: 21]. ﴿Say: "No one can protect me from Allah, nor will I find any refuge besides Him"﴾ [al-Jinn: 22], ﴿except a conveyance from Allah and His messages. And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, indeed, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn: 23]. ﴿Until, when they see what they are promised, they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number﴾ [al-Jinn: 24]. ﴿Say: "I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will set for it a long term"﴾ [al-Jinn: 25]. ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone﴾ [al-Jinn: 26], ﴿except one whom He has approved of among messengers; indeed, He sends before him and behind him guards﴾ [al-Jinn: 27], ﴿so that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord. And He has encompassed what is with them and has enumerated everything in number﴾ [al-Jinn: 28].

This is part of what is revealed under ﴿It has been revealed to me﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]. The word ﴿أنْ﴾ (an) is the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy ﴿inna﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَقامُوا﴾ (istaqamu, "they remained upright") refers to the following. Al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Zayd ibn Aslam and Abu Mijlaz said: it refers to the words ﴿فَمَن أسْلَمَ﴾ (fa-man aslama, "whoever submits") [al-Jinn: 14], and "the path" (al-tariqa) is the path of disbelief; that is, if those among the people who had submitted had disbelieved, ﴿لَأسْقَيْناهُمْ﴾ (la-asqaynahum, "We would have given them drink"), as a respite and gradual enticement for them. Using "uprightness" (istiqama) as a metaphor (isti'ara) for disbelief is strained and does not fit. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Jubayr said: it refers to the unjust (al-qasitin), and the meaning is that the path is Islam and truth; ﴿لَأنْعَمْنا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ (la-an'amna 'alayhim, "We would have bestowed favour upon them"), like His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ أنَّ أهْلَ الكِتابِ آمَنُوا واتَّقَوْا﴾ ("And if the People of the Book had believed and feared Allah") [al-Ma'ida: 65], and so on. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَقامُوا﴾ refers to all creation, and ﴿أنْ﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy one.

﴿لَأسْقَيْناهم ماءً غَدَقًا﴾ (la-asqaynahum ma'an ghadaqan, "We would have given them abundant water"): this is a metonymy (kinaya) for the widening of provision, since water is the basis of livelihood. Some said: wealth is where water is. The majority read ﴿غَدَقًا﴾ (ghadaqan) with a fatha on the dal; 'Asim, in the narration of al-A'sha, read it with a kasra. It is said: "the spring flowed abundantly (ghadaqat al-'ayn yughdiqu ghadaqan), so it is ghadiqa," when its water is plentiful. ﴿لِنَفْتِنَهم فِيهِ﴾ (li-naftinahum fihi, "so that We may test them therein"): that is, to test them as to how they will be thankful for what has been bestowed upon them, or to try them and gradually lead them on; and this depends on the disagreement about whom the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَقامُوا﴾ refers to.

Al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read the ﴿و﴾ of ﴿لَوِ﴾ (law) with a damma. The majority read it with a kasra. The Kufans read ﴿يَسْلُكْهُ﴾ (yaslukhu, "He will make him enter") with the ya', and the rest of the seven read it with the nun. Ibn Jundub read it with the nun from aslaka, and some of the Successors (al-tabi'un) read it with the ya' from aslaka as well. Both are dialects: salaka and aslaka. The poet said:

"Until, when they made them enter into Qutaʼida..."

The majority read ﴿صَعَدًا﴾ (sa'adan) with two fathas. It is a verbal noun (dhu masdar) of "sa'ida", used as a description of the punishment; that is, it overpowers the one being punished and dominates him. It was explained as "hardship (shaqq)". It is said: "So-and-so is in sa'ad of his affair", meaning in hardship. 'Umar said: "Nothing weighs on me (yutasa''adu bi) as much as what weighs on me in the marriage sermon," meaning: nothing is burdensome to me. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn 'Abbas said: "ṣaʻad" is a mountain in the Fire. Al-Khudri said: whenever they put their hands upon it, it melts. 'Ikrima said: it is a smooth rock in Hell which one is required to climb; when he reaches its top, he is sent down into Hell. According to this, it may be a substitute (badal) for ﴿عَذابًا﴾ ('adhaban) by omitting a qualifier, meaning "a punishment of ṣaʻad". It may also be that ﴿صَعَدًا﴾ is the object of ﴿يَسْلُكْهُ﴾, and ﴿عَذابًا﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). Some read ﴿صُعُدًا﴾ (su'udan) with two dammas; Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan read it with a damma on the sad and a fatha on the 'ayn. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is that there is no rest in it.

The majority read ﴿وأنَّ المَساجِدَ﴾ (wa-anna al-masajida, "and that the mosques") with a fatha on the hamza, as a coordination (ʻatf) with ﴿أنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ﴾ (annahu istama'a, "that it was he who listened") [al-Jinn: 1], so it is part of what is revealed. Al-Khalil said: the meaning of the verse is "and that the mosques belong to Allah, so do not invoke"; that is, for this reason. Similarly, in his view, ﴿لِإيلافِ قُرَيْشٍ﴾ (li-ilaf Quraysh) [Quraysh: 1] means "so let them worship" (fa-l-ya'budu), and likewise ﴿وأنَّ هَذِهِ أُمَتُّكم﴾ ("and that this your community") means "and because this" (wa-li-anna hadhihi). Ibn Harmaz and Talha read ﴿وإنَّ المَساجِدَ﴾ with a kasra, as a new sentence (isti'naf) and according to al-Khalil's reading; so the meaning is: do not invoke anyone alongside Allah in the mosques, because they belong to Allah alone and are for His worship. The apparent meaning is that the mosques are the houses prepared for prayer and worship in every religious community. Al-Hasan said: every place where prostration is performed is a mosque, whether it was specifically set aside for that or not, because the whole earth is a mosque for this community. Ibn 'Ata' went too far in saying that they are the limbs upon which one prostrates, whose singular is masjad with a fatha on the jim: the forehead, the nose, the two hands, the two knees and the two feet, counting the forehead and nose as one. Also too far is the one who said: "al-Masjid al-Haram", because it is the qibla of mosques, and he said that it is the plural of masjid meaning prostration. It is narrated that it was revealed when Quraysh had overcome the Ka'ba, and it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "All places belong to Allah, so worship Him wherever you are." Ibn Jubayr said: it was revealed because the jinn said: "O Messenger of Allah, how can we attend the prayer with you when we are far from you?" So the verse was revealed to address them with the meaning that your worship is accepted wherever you are, when we enter the mosques.

The majority read ﴿وأنَّهُ لَمّا قامَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ﴾ (wa-annahu lamma qama 'abdu Allah, "and that when the servant of Allah stood") with a fatha on the hamza, as a coordination with their reading ﴿وأنَّ المَساجِدَ﴾ with a fatha. Ibn Harmaz, Talha, Nafi' and Abu Bakr read it with a kasra as a new sentence. ʻAbd Allah is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿يَدْعُوهُ﴾ (yad'uhu, "calling upon Him") means calling upon Allah. ﴿كادُوا﴾ (kadu, "they almost") means the jinn almost. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: they were about to fall upon him to hear the Qur'an. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, in their gathering to reject his message. Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is that this is the saying of the jinn to their people, relating it; and the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾ refers to his companions who followed him and were bound to him in prayer. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why was it not said 'the Messenger of Allah' or 'the Prophet'?" I answer: because its implied meaning is: "And it was revealed to me that when the servant of Allah stood..." and since it occurs within the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about himself, it was phrased in a way that suits humility and self-abasement. Or because the meaning is that the worship of the servant of Allah to Allah is not something far-fetched from reason, nor something so objectionable that they should press upon him in opposition. The meaning of "stood calling upon Him" is "stood worshipping Him," meaning his standing for the dawn prayer at Nakhla when the jinn came to him and listened to his recitation, peace be upon him.

﴿كادُوا يَكُونُونَ عَلَيْهِ لِبَدًا﴾ (kadu yakununa 'alayhi libadan, "they almost became a crowd pressing upon him"): that is, they crowded around him piled upon one another, in wonder at what they saw of his worship and of his companions following him standing, bowing and prostrating, and in admiration of what he recited of the Qur'an, because they saw what they had never seen the like of and heard what they had never heard the like of. End of quotation. This is an earlier view which al-Zamakhshari embellished with his rhetoric. The majority read ﴿لِبَدًا﴾ (libadan) with a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the ba', the plural of libda, like kisra and kisar, meaning groups, likened to a thing matted with parts piled upon one another. From this is the verse of 'Abd Manaf ibn Rib':

"They lined up with six and four hundred tents, until it was as if upon them there was a side (of a crowd) matted together."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "a'wanan" (helpers). Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn 'Amir, in one narration from him, read it with a damma on the lam, the plural of lubda, like zubra and zubur. Also from Ibn Muhaysin: sukun on the ba' and damma on the lam (lubdan). Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Abu Hayya and a group from Abu 'Amr read it with two dammas, as the plural of labd, like rahn and ruhn, or as the plural of labud, like sabur and subur. Al-Hasan and al-Jahdari, in one narration from each, read it (libbadan) with a damma on the lam and a shadda on the ba' with a fatha. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: when the Messenger stood to call, the humans and jinn matted together against this matter to extinguish it, but Allah refused except to give him victory and perfect His light. End of quotation. Those who said that 'Abd Allah here is Nuh (peace be upon him), whose people almost killed him until Allah rescued him from them, were far off the mark; this was said by al-Hasan. Even further off is the view that it is 'Abd Allah ibn Salam.

The majority read: ﴿قالَ إنَّما أدْعُو رَبِّي﴾ (qala innama ad'u rabbi, "He said: I only invoke my Lord"); that is, he said to those who were gathered against him: ﴿إنَّما أدْعُو رَبِّي﴾ ("I only invoke my Lord"), meaning: I have not come to you with a thing to be denied; I only worship my Lord alone, and this is not what should make you unite in enmity against me. Or he said to the jinn, who were crowding in wonder: what you see of the worship of Allah is not a matter to be wondered at; rather, wonder is for one who worships other than Him. Or the jinn said to their people, relating what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said; all of this follows from the disagreement over the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾. ʻAsim, Hamza and Abu 'Amr, in one narration from him, read: ﴿قُلْ﴾ (qul, "Say"); that is, say, O Muhammad, to these who crowd around you, who are either the jinn or the polytheists, according to the two views about the pronoun in ﴿كادُوا﴾.

Then Allah commanded him to say to them what shows his disclaimer of the power to bring them any benefit or harm, and He made harm (darr) the counterpart of right guidance (rushd), expressing by it misguidance (ghayy), since misguidance's result is harm. The meaning may be: harm and no benefit, nor misguidance nor right guidance, so that from each he omitted the counterpart of what indicates it. Al-A'raj read ﴿رُشُدًا﴾ (rushudan) with two dammas. When he (peace be upon him) disclaimed his power to benefit or harm them, he was commanded to inform them that he is a creature (marbub) of Allah Most High, whose Lord does what He wills with him, and that no one can protect him from Him, nor will he find any refuge other than Him to lean upon. Qatada said something close to this. Al-Suddi said: a shelter (hirz). Al-Kalbi said: an entrance into the earth. It was also said: a helper; and it was said: a way and a path, and from this is the poet's saying:

"Alas for my soul! And my soul is of no use to me, and there is no refuge (multahad) from Allah's decree."

It was also said: there is an omission in the speech, which is: they said to him, leave what you call to, and we will protect you; so it was said to him: say, "No one can protect me." It was also said: it is a reply to the words of Wardan, the chief of the jinn, when they were crowded around him: Wardan said, "I will remove them from you," and he said, "No one can protect me," as mentioned by al-Mawardi.

﴿إلّا بَلاغًا﴾ (illa balaghan, "except a conveyance") [al-Jinn: 23]: al-Hasan said: this is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: no one can protect me, but if I convey the message, He will show mercy to me through it. The "protection" (ijara) for conveyance is metaphorical (musta'ara), since it is the cause of Allah's protection and mercy. It was also said that, according to this meaning, it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), meaning: no one can protect me concerning anyone, but I have found nothing to incline to and to hold to except that I convey and obey, so that Allah protects me. So it is permissible to put it in the accusative as an exception from (multahadan), and as a substitute (badal), which is the better view, because what precedes it is a negation; al-Zajjaj construed it as a substitute. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: this exception is disjunctive, because he did not say "and I will not find a refuge," rather he said "besides Him," and conveyance from Allah does not fall under His saying "a refuge besides Him," because it does not come from beside Allah, but from Allah and by His help and His guidance. Qatada said: the implied meaning is: I possess nothing except conveying to you; as for faith and disbelief, I do not possess them. End of quotation. This has a distance to it because of the long separation between the two. It was also said that ﴿إلّا﴾ (illa), in the sense of separation, is: "in" (conditional) and "la" (negative), and its verb is omitted because the verbal noun indicates it; the meaning is: if I do not convey a conveyance from Allah and His message. This is like your saying: "in la qiyaman qu'udan," meaning: if you do not stand in standing, then sit in sitting. The omission of this verb may be because of an indication of it after or before it, as it is omitted in the poet's saying:

"Divorce her, for you are not a match for her, and if not, the sword will reach your forehead."

The estimate: "And if you do not divorce her," where "do not divorce her" (tuṭalliqhā) is omitted because of the indication of "fa-ṭalliqhā" (so divorce her) upon it, and "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya).

Al-Zamakhshari said, following Qatada: meaning, I do not possess [any power] except a conveyance (balāghan) from Allah. And "Say: Indeed, none will protect me from Allah" is a parenthetical sentence (jumla muʿtarida) which he inserted to emphasise the negation of capability from himself and to show his powerlessness, in the sense that: if Allah intends harm to him, such as sickness, death or other than these two, no one can protect him from it, nor find besides Him a refuge to which he may take shelter. End of quote.

(wa-risālātihi) It has been said: it is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "balāghan," meaning: except that I convey from Allah, or I convey His messages. The apparent meaning is that "wa-risālātihi" is a conjunction upon "Allah," meaning: except that I convey from Allah and from His messages.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 72, verses 23–28 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾: that is, by associating partners with Allah and by disbelief. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read (fa-inna lahu) with a kasra on the hamza. Talha read it with a fatha, and the implied construction is: "fa-jaza'uhu anna lahu" (then his recompense is that for him). Ibn Khalawayh said: "I heard Ibn Mujahid say: No one read it this way, and it is a grammatical error (lahn), because it comes after the fa' of the conditional." I also heard Ibn al-Anbari say: "It is an accepted form (dirab), and its meaning is: then his recompense is that for him is the fire of Hell." End of quotation. Ibn Mujahid was an imam in the qira'at (canonical Qur'anic readings), but he did not have a wide range of transmitted readings the way Ibn Shanabudh did, and he was weak in grammar (nahw). How can he say that no one read it this way, when Talha ibn Musarrif did read it this way? And how can he say that it is an error, when the grammarians have explicitly stated that inna after the fa' of the conditional may be read with either a fatha or a kasra?

He used the plural (khalidin) in agreement with the meaning of (man) ("whoever"), after having used the singular form of (man) in agreement with its wording in His saying (yaʿṣi, "disobeys") and (fa-inna lahu, "then for him").

﴿Until, when they see﴾: (hatta) here is a particle of initiation (harf ibtida'), meaning that it may be followed by a nominal sentence (jumlat al-ibtida' wa-l-khabar), while it also carries the sense of a limit or endpoint (al-ghayah). Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what does (hatta) relate to, such that what follows it is its endpoint? I answer: it relates to His saying ﴿they will be against him as a mass﴾ [al-Jinn: 19], in the sense that they band together against him in enmity, belittle his helpers, and consider their number insignificant, ﴿until, when they see what they are promised﴾ from the Day of Badr and Allah's giving him victory over them, or from the Day of Resurrection. Then they will know at that time that they are ﴿weaker in helpers and fewer in number﴾." It may also relate to an implied element indicated by the state of the disbelievers' belittling of him and their considering his followers few, as if to say: they continue in what they are doing, ﴿until, when they see what they are promised﴾. The disbelievers said: "When will this promised thing happen?" as a denial of it. It was said to them: "Say: it is certainly coming, there is no doubt about it, so do not deny it. Allah has promised it, and He does not break His promise. As for its time, I do not know when it will be, because Allah has not revealed it, given the benefit He sees in keeping its time hidden." End of quotation.

As for his saying: "What does (in) relate to?" he meant the relation of a particle of jarr (preposition), and this is not correct, because (hatta) here is a particle of initiation, so what follows it is not in a position of jarr (genitive case). This differs from the view of al-Zajjaj and Ibn Darastawayh, who claimed that when it is a particle of initiation, the initiating sentence after it is in a position of jarr. If by "relating" he meant the connection of what follows to what precedes, and that what follows is the endpoint of what precedes, then that is correct. As for his claim that it relates to His saying ﴿they will be against him as a mass﴾ [al-Jinn: 19], that is very remote, because of the long separation between them by many sentences.

Al-Tibrizi said: "(hatta) may serve as an endpoint for an implied element," but he did not specify what the implied element is. It was also said: the meaning is, "Leave them until, when they see what they are promised of the Hour, ﴿they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number﴾: whether they or the People of the Book?" What appears to me is that it is an endpoint for what the preceding sentence contains of the judgment that the fire will be their dwelling. It is as if it were said: the one who disobeys is judged to have the fire as his dwelling, and this judgment is a threat, until, when they see what they were judged to dwell in, ﴿they will know﴾. So His saying ﴿then for him is the fire of Hell﴾ is a threat to them with the Fire. And ﴿who is weaker﴾ is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate) in a position of nasb (accusative) governed by what precedes it, and it is mu'allaq (suspended), because (man) is an interrogative. It is also permissible for (man) to be a relative pronoun in a position of nasb governed by (sa-ya'lamun, "they will know"), with (adʿaf, "weaker") being the khabar of an omitted mubtada'. The sentence is then the relative clause of (man), its estimate being: "he is weaker." Its omission is acceptable because the relative clause is long, with the object (nasiran, "helpers") intervening.

Makhul said: "This was revealed only concerning the jinn. Among them, whoever was granted success embraced Islam, and whoever was forsaken disbelieved, just as among humans." He said: "The number of those who followed the Prophet ﷺ on the night of the jinn reached seventy thousand, and they were alarmed at the breaking of dawn." Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to tell them that he does not know the time of the long duration of what they were promised, whether it is near or far.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿Or will my Lord set for it a term?﴾ when a term may be near or far? Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿she would wish that between her and it were a long distance﴾ [Al 'Imran: 30]?" I answer: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to consider the appointed time to be near, so it is as if he said: "I do not know whether it is a condition that is expected at every hour, or a deferred matter for which an end has been set." That is, He is the Knower of the unseen.

﴿So He does not reveal﴾: so He does not disclose. And (min rasul, "of a messenger") is an explanation of (man irtada, "whom He has chosen"). The meaning is that none discloses the unseen except one chosen who is selected for prophethood specifically, not every chosen person. In this there is a refutation of miracles (karamat), because those who are attributed such things, even if they are chosen saints (awliya' murtadin), are not messengers. Allah has singled out the messengers from among the chosen by disclosure of the unseen and by refuting soothsaying (kihana) and astrology (tanjim), because their practitioners are the furthest of all things from being chosen and the most deserving of anger. End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾. Al-Hasan said: it is what is hidden from His creation. It was said: it is the Hour. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: (illa, "except") means (lakin, "but"), so he treated it as an exception that is disconnected (istithna' munqati'). It was also said: (illa) means (wa-la, "and not"), that is: "and not whom He has chosen from among the messengers." And (ʿalim, "Knower") is the khabar of an omitted mubtada', meaning "He is the Knower of the unseen," or it is a badal (substitute) for (rabbi, "my Lord"). It was read (ʿalliman) with a fatha, as praise (madh). Al-Suddi said: (ʿalima al-ghayb) as a past verb governing (al-ghayb) as its object. The majority read (ʿalimu al-ghayb) as an active participle (ism fa'il) in the nominative case. The majority read (fa-la yuzhiru) from (azhara). Al-Hasan read (yazhar) with a fatha on the ya' and the ha', from (zahara).

﴿Except whom He has chosen from a messenger﴾: this is an exception from (ahadan, "anyone"), meaning: then He discloses to him what He wills of that. He causes to walk before that messenger and behind him ﴿watchers﴾, meaning guardians who protect him from the jinn and guard him in securing what Allah conveys to that messenger of the knowledge of the unseen. From al-Dahhak: No prophet was ever sent without angels accompanying him to guard him from the devils, lest they appear in the form of an angel.

Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars said: When Allah, exalted is He, praised Himself with knowledge of the unseen and reserved it for Himself to the exclusion of His creation, this is evidence that no one other than Him knows the unseen. Then He excepted whom He chose from among the messengers, and He deposited in them what He willed of His unseen knowledge through revelation to them, making it a miracle for them and a true sign of their prophethood. Then he mentioned, as evidence, the refutation of what the astrologer (munajjim) claims, and then he permitted the shedding of the astrologer's blood. Al-Wahidi said: In this is evidence that whoever claims that the stars indicate what will happen, whether of life, death, or other things, has disbelieved in what is in the Qur'an.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi and al-Wahidi said: Miracles (karamat) are permissible, according to what the author of al-Kashshaf said. He understood them as indicating the prevention of judgments by astrology, and not as indicating inspirations, which are merely a kind of resemblance. In my view, however, the verse does not indicate anything of what they have said, because His saying ﴿upon His unseen﴾ contains no element of generality, so it suffices in acting upon its requirement that Allah not disclose to any of His creation a single one of His unseen matters. It is to be understood as referring to the time of the establishment of the Resurrection, so there remains no evidence in the verse that He does not disclose any of the unseen to anyone. This is reinforced by the fact that He mentioned this verse immediately after His saying ﴿I do not know whether what you are promised is near or whether my Lord will set for it a term﴾, meaning: I do not know the time of the occurrence of the Resurrection, since it is part of the unseen which Allah does not disclose to anyone. And ﴿except whom He has chosen﴾ is a disconnected exception, as if He said: He does not disclose His specific unseen to anyone, except whom He has chosen from among the messengers, for whom there are guardians who protect him from the evil of the rebellious among humans and jinn.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: You should know that it is necessary to affirm with certainty that the intended meaning of this verse is not that no one at all can know any of the unseen things except the messengers, peace be upon them. What indicates this are several points. The first: it has been established by reports close to mutawatir (widely transmitted) that Shiq and Sati' were two soothsayers who foretold the emergence of Muhammad ﷺ before the time of his emergence. They were famous among the Arabs for this kind of knowledge, to the extent that Kisra sent for them to learn about the news of our Messenger, ﷺ. The second: the consensus of the nations on the validity of the science of ta'bir (dream interpretation), whereby the interpreter informs of what will happen in the future and is truthful. The third: the Baghdadi soothsayer whom Sultan Sanjar ibn Malikshah brought from Baghdad to Khurasan asked her about things in the future, and she informed of them and they occurred according to her words. I have quoted this man's words on this question only so that we may examine the points he mentioned. As for the story of Shiq and Sati', there is nothing in it of foretelling the unseen, because it is among what the spirit (ra'iy) of the soothsayers from the devils reports, stealing hearing, as came in the hadith: "They hear the word, and they lie, and they throw it to the soothsayers, and the soothsayers add a hundred lies to the word." Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 72, verses 23–28 (part 2 of 2)

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (li-ya'lama) with the verb in the active voice. Qatadah said: "That Muhammad (ﷺ) may know that the messengers have indeed conveyed the messages of their Lord and kept them safe." Ibn Jubayr said: "That Muhammad may know that the guardian angels (al-hafazah al-rusad), who descend before and behind Jibril, have indeed conveyed the messages of their Lord." Mujahid said: "That whoever associated partners with God and denied (the message) may know that the messengers did convey it, and according to this view, this knowledge will not occur for them except in the Hereafter." It was also said: "That God may know His messengers as conveyers, brought out into existence, since His knowledge of everything has already preceded." Al-Zamakhshari chose this last view and said: "(That God may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord): he means the prophets." He used the singular first in the words ﴿from before him and from behind him﴾ according to the wording, then used the plural according to the meaning, as in His words ﴿for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein﴾, and the meaning is: that they may convey the messages of their Lord as they are, guarded from addition and deficiency. He mentioned knowledge in the manner of His saying ﴿until We know the strivers﴾ [Muhammad: 31]. End of quotation. It was also said: "(li-ya'lama)" means: which messenger it was that the other messengers had conveyed (the message) before him. It was said: "That Iblis may know that the messengers have conveyed the messages of their Lord unadulterated by his confusion and the excesses of his companions." It was said: "That the messengers may know that the angels have conveyed the messages of their Lord." It was said: "That Muhammad may know that Jibril and those with him have conveyed to him the message of his Lord." It was said: "That the jinn may know that the messengers have conveyed what was sent down to them, and that they were not the ones receiving it by eavesdropping."

Ibn Abbas and Zayd ibn Ali read (li-yu'lama) with a damma on the ya' and the verb in the passive voice. Al-Zuhri and Ibn Abi Ablah read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the lam, meaning: "That God may make known" (li-yu'lima Allah), i.e., to whomever He wills to make Him know, that the messengers have conveyed His messages.

The majority read (risalat) in the plural. Abu Haywah read it in the singular.

The majority read ﴿wa-ahāta bi-mā ladayhim﴾ with ahāta in the active voice, meaning God, and (wa-ahsā) in the active voice, meaning God, with (kulla) in the accusative. Ibn Abi Ablah read (wa-uḥīṭa) and (wa-uḥṣiya) in the passive voice, with (kullu) in the nominative. Since li-ya'lama was implicitly containing the meaning of 'alima, the meaning becomes: "He has indeed known that," so the clause wa-ahāta is coordinated with this pronoun. The meaning is: He encompassed what the messengers had of wisdom and laws, nothing of them escaping Him.

﴿And He has counted everything in number﴾: that is, numbered and enumerated. Its being in the accusative is as a circumstantial state (hal) from (kulla shay'), even though it is indefinite, because the definite is included in the generality. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar) of (ahsā), since it carries the meaning of ihsa'. Abu al-Baqa said: "It is also permissible for it to be a specifier (tamyiz)." End of quotation, and then it would be transferred from the object, since its original form would be: "and He counted the number of every thing." Whether this usage is established in the language of the Arabs is a matter of disagreement.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 72, verses 23–28 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾: that is, by associating partners with Allah and by disbelief. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾.

He used the plural (khalidin) in agreement with the meaning of (man) ("whoever"), after having used the singular form of (man) in agreement with its wording in His saying (yaʿṣi, "disobeys") and (fa-inna lahu, "then for him").

He said: "The number of those who followed the Prophet ﷺ on the night of the jinn reached seventy thousand, and they were alarmed at the breaking of dawn." The meaning is that none discloses the unseen except one chosen who is selected for prophethood specifically, not every chosen person. In this there is a refutation of miracles (karamat), because those who are attributed such things, even if they are chosen saints (awliya' murtadin), are not messengers. Allah has singled out the messengers from among the chosen by disclosure of the unseen and by refuting soothsaying (kihana) and astrology (tanjim), because their practitioners are the furthest of all things from being chosen and the most deserving of anger. End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾. Al-Hasan said: it is what is hidden from His creation. It was said: it is the Hour. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: (illa, "except") means (lakin, "but"), so he treated it as an exception that is disconnected (istithna' munqati'). It was also said: (illa) means (wa-la, "and not"), that is: "and not whom He has chosen from among the messengers." And (ʿalim, "Knower") is the khabar of an omitted mubtada', meaning "He is the Knower of the unseen," or it is a badal (substitute) for (rabbi, "my Lord"). It was read (ʿalliman) with a fatha, as praise (madh). Al-Suddi said: (ʿalima al-ghayb) as a past verb governing (al-ghayb) as its object. The majority read (ʿalimu al-ghayb) as an active participle (ism fa'il) in the nominative case. The majority read (fa-la yuzhiru) from (azhara). Al-Hasan read (yazhar) with a fatha on the ya' and the ha', from (zahara).

It was also said: the meaning is, "Leave them until, when they see what they are promised of the Hour, ﴿they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number﴾: whether they or the People of the Book?" What appears to me is that it is an endpoint for what the preceding sentence contains of the judgment that the fire will be their dwelling. It is as if it were said: the one who disobeys is judged to have the fire as his dwelling, and this judgment is a threat, until, when they see what they were judged to dwell in, ﴿they will know﴾. So His saying ﴿then for him is the fire of Hell﴾ is a threat to them with the Fire. And ﴿who is weaker﴾ is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate) in a position of nasb (accusative) governed by what precedes it, and it is mu'allaq (suspended), because (man) is an interrogative. It is also permissible for (man) to be a relative pronoun in a position of nasb governed by (sa-ya'lamun, "they will know"), with (adʿaf, "weaker") being the khabar of an omitted mubtada'. The sentence is then the relative clause of (man), its estimate being: "he is weaker." Its omission is acceptable because the relative clause is long, with the object (nasiran, "helpers") intervening.

Makhul said: "This was revealed only concerning the jinn. Among them, whoever was granted success embraced Islam, and whoever was forsaken disbelieved, just as among humans." He said: "The number of those who followed the Prophet ﷺ on the night of the jinn reached seventy thousand, and they were alarmed at the breaking of dawn." Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to tell them that he does not know the time of the long duration of what they were promised, whether it is near or far.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿Or will my Lord set for it a term?﴾ when a term may be near or far? That is, He is the Knower of the unseen.

﴿So He does not reveal﴾: so He does not disclose. And (min rasul, "of a messenger") is an explanation of (man irtada, "whom He has chosen"). End of quotation.

So we say: the correct interpretation is what we have mentioned. End of quotation, with some abridgment.

﴿And He has counted everything in number﴾: that is, numbered and enumerated. Abu al-Baqa said: "It is also permissible for it to be a specifier (tamyiz)." End of quotation, and then it would be transferred from the object, since its original form would be: "and He counted the number of every thing." Whether this usage is established in the language of the Arabs is a matter of disagreement.

Al-Zuhri and Ibn Abi Ablah read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the lam, meaning: "That God may make known" (li-yu'lima Allah), i.e., to whomever He wills to make Him know, that the messengers have conveyed His messages.

The meaning is: He encompassed what the messengers had of wisdom and laws, nothing of them escaping Him.

﴿And He has counted everything in number﴾: that is, numbered and enumerated. Its being in the accusative is as a circumstantial state (hal) from (kulla shay'), even though it is indefinite, because the definite is included in the generality. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar) of (ahsā), since it carries the meaning of ihsa'. Abu al-Baqa said: "It is also permissible for it to be a specifier (tamyiz)." End of quotation, and then it would be transferred from the object, since its original form would be: "and He counted the number of every thing." Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 72, verses 23–28 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾: that is, by associating partners with Allah and by disbelief. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾.

End of quotation.

It was also said: the meaning is, "Leave them until, when they see what they are promised of the Hour, ﴿they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number﴾: whether they or the People of the Book?" What appears to me is that it is an endpoint for what the preceding sentence contains of the judgment that the fire will be their dwelling. It is as if it were said: the one who disobeys is judged to have the fire as his dwelling, and this judgment is a threat, until, when they see what they were judged to dwell in, ﴿they will know﴾. So His saying ﴿then for him is the fire of Hell﴾ is a threat to them with the Fire. And ﴿who is weaker﴾ is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate) in a position of nasb (accusative) governed by what precedes it, and it is mu'allaq (suspended), because (man) is an interrogative. It is also permissible for (man) to be a relative pronoun in a position of nasb governed by (sa-ya'lamun, "they will know"), with (adʿaf, "weaker") being the khabar of an omitted mubtada'. The sentence is then the relative clause of (man), its estimate being: "he is weaker." Makhul said: "This was revealed only concerning the jinn. Among them, whoever was granted success embraced Islam, and whoever was forsaken disbelieved, just as among humans." He said: "The number of those who followed the Prophet ﷺ on the night of the jinn reached seventy thousand, and they were alarmed at the breaking of dawn." Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to tell them that he does not know the time of the long duration of what they were promised, whether it is near or far.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿Or will my Lord set for it a term?﴾ when a term may be near or far? ﴿So He does not reveal﴾: so He does not disclose. And (min rasul, "of a messenger") is an explanation of (man irtada, "whom He has chosen"). End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾. Al-Hasan said: it is what is hidden from His creation. It was said: it is the Hour. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: (illa, "except") means (lakin, "but"), so he treated it as an exception that is disconnected (istithna' munqati'). It was also said: (illa) means (wa-la, "and not"), that is: "and not whom He has chosen from among the messengers." The majority read (ʿalimu al-ghayb) as an active participle (ism fa'il) in the nominative case. The majority read (fa-la yuzhiru) from (azhara). Al-Hasan read (yazhar) with a fatha on the ya' and the ha', from (zahara).

From al-Dahhak: No prophet was ever sent without angels accompanying him to guard him from the devils, lest they appear in the form of an angel.

Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars said: When Allah, exalted is He, praised Himself with knowledge of the unseen and reserved it for Himself to the exclusion of His creation, this is evidence that no one other than Him knows the unseen. Then He excepted whom He chose from among the messengers, and He deposited in them what He willed of His unseen knowledge through revelation to them, making it a miracle for them and a true sign of their prophethood. Then he mentioned, as evidence, the refutation of what the astrologer (munajjim) claims, and then he permitted the shedding of the astrologer's blood. Al-Wahidi said: In this is evidence that whoever claims that the stars indicate what will happen, whether of life, death, or other things, has disbelieved in what is in the Qur'an.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi and al-Wahidi said: Miracles (karamat) are permissible, according to what the author of al-Kashshaf said. He understood them as indicating the prevention of judgments by astrology, and not as indicating inspirations, which are merely a kind of resemblance. It is to be understood as referring to the time of the establishment of the Resurrection, so there remains no evidence in the verse that He does not disclose any of the unseen to anyone. This is reinforced by the fact that He mentioned this verse immediately after His saying ﴿I do not know whether what you are promised is near or whether my Lord will set for it a term﴾, meaning: I do not know the time of the occurrence of the Resurrection, since it is part of the unseen which Allah does not disclose to anyone. And ﴿except whom He has chosen﴾ is a disconnected exception, as if He said: He does not disclose His specific unseen to anyone, except whom He has chosen from among the messengers, for whom there are guardians who protect him from the evil of the rebellious among humans and jinn.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: You should know that it is necessary to affirm with certainty that the intended meaning of this verse is not that no one at all can know any of the unseen things except the messengers, peace be upon them. What indicates this are several points. The first: it has been established by reports close to mutawatir (widely transmitted) that Shiq and Sati' were two soothsayers who foretold the emergence of Muhammad ﷺ before the time of his emergence. They were famous among the Arabs for this kind of knowledge, to the extent that Kisra sent for them to learn about the news of our Messenger, ﷺ. The second: the consensus of the nations on the validity of the science of ta'bir (dream interpretation), whereby the interpreter informs of what will happen in the future and is truthful. The third: the Baghdadi soothsayer whom Sultan Sanjar ibn Malikshah brought from Baghdad to Khurasan asked her about things in the future, and she informed of them and they occurred according to her words. I have seen people who are scholars of kalam and philosophy who reported from her that she informed of unseen things in detail, and that they came about as she said. Abu al-Barakat, author of al-Mu'tabar, exaggerated in describing her condition in the book on interpretation, and said: I investigated her condition for thirty years until I became certain that she used to report unseen things with accurate and agreeing reports. The fourth: we observe people with true inspirations. This is not restricted to the saints. Among sorcerers and in astrological judgments there is also what agrees with truth, though lying occurs among them much more often. When this is observed and perceived, the claim that the Qur'an indicates the opposite leads to casting doubt upon the Qur'an, and that is false. So we say: the correct interpretation is what we have mentioned. End of quotation, with some abridgment.

I have quoted this man's words on this question only so that we may examine the points he mentioned. As for the story of Shiq and Sati', there is nothing in it of foretelling the unseen, because it is among what the spirit (ra'iy) of the soothsayers from the devils reports, stealing hearing, as came in the hadith: "They hear the word, and they lie, and they throw it to the soothsayers, and the soothsayers add a hundred lies to the word." This is not from the knowledge of the unseen, since the word was spoken by the angels, and the jinni snatched it, and the soothsayer snatched it from him. So the soothsayer did not know the unseen. As for interpreting dreams, the interpreter who is not infallible does not interpret by way of certainty and decisiveness, but by way of conjecture and estimation, and what he interprets may happen or may not happen. As for the Baghdadi soothsayer and what is reported of her, it is enough for intellect to reason from the condition of a woman whom he did not witness. Even if he had witnessed it, his intellect could allow that he was deceived about it, and he is the scholar and author whose fame reached the horizons, and who cast doubt on the proofs of the philosophers and overwhelmed them. As for his report from the author of al-Mu'tabar, that man was a Jew who displayed Islam while adopting the method of the philosophers. As for his witnessing those with true inspirations, I have been about seventy-three years of age, accompanying scholars and frequenting those who are attributed to righteousness, and I have not seen any of them with a true inspiration. As for miracles, I have no doubt that some of them occur, but this is rare, and it occurs among the righteous of this nation who have passed. It may be that in our times there are some from whom miracles proceed, and Allah, exalted is He, may single out whom He wills with what He wills. And Allah is the Granter of success.

This is reinforced by the fact that He mentioned this verse immediately after His saying ﴿I do not know whether what you are promised is near or whether my Lord will set for it a term﴾, meaning: I do not know the time of the occurrence of the Resurrection, since it is part of the unseen which Allah does not disclose to anyone. And ﴿except whom He has chosen﴾ is a disconnected exception, as if He said: He does not disclose His specific unseen to anyone, except whom He has chosen from among the messengers, for whom there are guardians who protect him from the evil of the rebellious among humans and jinn.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: You should know that it is necessary to affirm with certainty that the intended meaning of this verse is not that no one at all can know any of the unseen things except the messengers, peace be upon them. What indicates this are several points. The first: it has been established by reports close to mutawatir (widely transmitted) that Shiq and Sati' were two soothsayers who foretold the emergence of Muhammad ﷺ before the time of his emergence. They were famous among the Arabs for this kind of knowledge, to the extent that Kisra sent for them to learn about the news of our Messenger, ﷺ. The second: the consensus of the nations on the validity of the science of ta'bir (dream interpretation), whereby the interpreter informs of what will happen in the future and is truthful. The third: the Baghdadi soothsayer whom Sultan Sanjar ibn Malikshah brought from Baghdad to Khurasan asked her about things in the future, and she informed of them and they occurred according to her words. I have seen people who are scholars of kalam and philosophy who reported from her that she informed of unseen things in detail, and that they came about as she said. Abu al-Barakat, author of al-Mu'tabar, exaggerated in describing her condition in the book on interpretation, and said: I investigated her condition for thirty years until I became certain that she used to report unseen things with accurate and agreeing reports. The fourth: we observe people with true inspirations. This is not restricted to the saints. Among sorcerers and in astrological judgments there is also what agrees with truth, though lying occurs among them much more often. When this is observed and perceived, the claim that the Qur'an indicates the opposite leads to casting doubt upon the Qur'an, and that is false. So we say: the correct interpretation is what we have mentioned. End of quotation, with some abridgment.

I have quoted this man's words on this question only so that we may examine the points he mentioned. As for the story of Shiq and Sati', there is nothing in it of foretelling the unseen, because it is among what the spirit (ra'iy) of the soothsayers from the devils reports, stealing hearing, as came in the hadith: "They hear the word, and they lie, and they throw it to the soothsayers, and the soothsayers add a hundred lies to the word." This is not from the knowledge of the unseen, since the word was spoken by the angels, and the jinni snatched it, and the soothsayer snatched it from him. So the soothsayer did not know the unseen. As for interpreting dreams, the interpreter who is not infallible does not interpret by way of certainty and decisiveness, but by way of conjecture and estimation, and what he interprets may happen or may not happen. As for the Baghdadi soothsayer and what is reported of her, it is enough for intellect to reason from the condition of a woman whom he did not witness. Even if he had witnessed it, his intellect could allow that he was deceived about it, and he is the scholar and author whose fame reached the horizons, and who cast doubt on the proofs of the philosophers and overwhelmed them. As for his report from the author of al-Mu'tabar, that man was a Jew who displayed Islam while adopting the method of the philosophers. As for his witnessing those with true inspirations, I have been about seventy-three years of age, accompanying scholars and frequenting those who are attributed to righteousness, and I have not seen any of them with a true inspiration. As for miracles, I have no doubt that some of them occur, but this is rare, and it occurs among the righteous of this nation who have passed. It may be that in our times there are some from whom miracles proceed, and Allah, exalted is He, may single out whom He wills with what He wills. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 72, verses 23–28 (part 2 of 2)

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (li-ya'lama) with the verb in the active voice. Qatadah said: "That Muhammad (ﷺ) may know that the messengers have indeed conveyed the messages of their Lord and kept them safe." Ibn Jubayr said: "That Muhammad may know that the guardian angels (al-hafazah al-rusad), who descend before and behind Jibril, have indeed conveyed the messages of their Lord." Mujahid said: "That whoever associated partners with God and denied (the message) may know that the messengers did convey it, and according to this view, this knowledge will not occur for them except in the Hereafter." It was also said: "That God may know His messengers as conveyers, brought out into existence, since His knowledge of everything has already preceded." Al-Zamakhshari chose this last view and said: "(That God may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord): he means the prophets." He used the singular first in the words ﴿from before him and from behind him﴾ according to the wording, then used the plural according to the meaning, as in His words ﴿for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein﴾, and the meaning is: that they may convey the messages of their Lord as they are, guarded from addition and deficiency. He mentioned knowledge in the manner of His saying ﴿until We know the strivers﴾ [Muhammad: 31]. End of quotation. It was also said: "(li-ya'lama)" means: which messenger it was that the other messengers had conveyed (the message) before him. It was said: "That Iblis may know that the messengers have conveyed the messages of their Lord unadulterated by his confusion and the excesses of his companions." It was said: "That the messengers may know that the angels have conveyed the messages of their Lord." It was said: "That Muhammad may know that Jibril and those with him have conveyed to him the message of his Lord." It was said: "That the jinn may know that the messengers have conveyed what was sent down to them, and that they were not the ones receiving it by eavesdropping."

Ibn Abbas and Zayd ibn Ali read (li-yu'lama) with a damma on the ya' and the verb in the passive voice. Al-Zuhri and Ibn Abi Ablah read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the lam, meaning: "That God may make known" (li-yu'lima Allah), i.e., to whomever He wills to make Him know, that the messengers have conveyed His messages.

The majority read (risalat) in the plural. Abu Haywah read it in the singular.

The majority read ﴿wa-ahāta bi-mā ladayhim﴾ with ahāta in the active voice, meaning God, and (wa-ahsā) in the active voice, meaning God, with (kulla) in the accusative. Ibn Abi Ablah read (wa-uḥīṭa) and (wa-uḥṣiya) in the passive voice, with (kullu) in the nominative. Since li-ya'lama was implicitly containing the meaning of 'alima, the meaning becomes: "He has indeed known that," so the clause wa-ahāta is coordinated with this pronoun. The meaning is: He encompassed what the messengers had of wisdom and laws, nothing of them escaping Him.

﴿And He has counted everything in number﴾: that is, numbered and enumerated. Its being in the accusative is as a circumstantial state (hal) from (kulla shay'), even though it is indefinite, because the definite is included in the generality. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar) of (ahsā), since it carries the meaning of ihsa'. Abu al-Baqa said: "It is also permissible for it to be a specifier (tamyiz)." End of quotation, and then it would be transferred from the object, since its original form would be: "and He counted the number of every thing." Whether this usage is established in the language of the Arabs is a matter of disagreement.
